weeks.title: Finance U1·W1 — Financial Statements, the Cash-Flow Statement & Taxes
weeks.lessonHtml:
Why a finance course starts with the statements

Corporate finance is the discipline of valuing and financing real decisions, and every valuation begins with numbers pulled from three financial statements: the income statement, the balance sheet, and the statement of cash flows. This week builds fluency in reading and constructing all three, plus the ratio toolkit (anchored by the DuPont identity) and the basics of corporate taxes. Our running fictional company is Meridian Building Group (MBG), a mid-size contractor, with Riverton Development and Northstar Services as comparison firms. Master's-level depth, but exam-focused: you must be able to move from a trial balance to finished statements and back to the ratios an analyst quotes.

The income statement — the standard ladder

The income statement is a top-to-bottom ladder. Memorize the order because exam problems give you a few lines and ask for one further down: Sales − COGS = Gross Profit (GP); GP − Operating Expenses (SG&A, depreciation) = EBIT (operating income); EBIT − Interest = EBT (pre-tax income); EBT − Taxes = Net Income (NI); and EPS = NI / shares outstanding. Worked example for Northstar Services: Sales $5,000,000; COGS $1,060,000 ⇒ GP $3,940,000; operating expenses $1,450,000 ⇒ EBIT $2,490,000; interest $300,000 ⇒ EBT $2,190,000; taxes at 30% = $657,000 ⇒ NI $1,533,000; with 500,000 shares, EPS = $3.07. Notice depreciation is an operating expense above EBIT — it is a non-cash charge that still reduces taxable income, which is why it reappears in cash-flow and tax analysis.

LIFO vs FIFO trap. COGS depends on the inventory cost-flow assumption. In a rising-price environment, FIFO leaves newer (higher) costs in ending inventory and pushes older (lower) costs to COGS, producing lower COGS, higher gross profit, and higher taxes. LIFO does the reverse: higher COGS, lower gross profit, lower taxes. Same physical goods, different reported profit — a classic conceptual question.

The balance sheet — assets = liabilities + equity

The balance sheet is a point-in-time snapshot satisfying Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory) and current liabilities (payables, accruals, short-term debt) drive liquidity; long-term assets (PP&E, net of accumulated depreciation) and long-term debt drive solvency. Equity = common stock + additional paid-in capital (APIC) + retained earnings. Retained earnings roll forward: RE(end) = RE(begin) + Net Income − Dividends. For MBG, construction work-in-progress (WIP) sits in current assets as an asset until a home closes — a finance student should recognize that an asset on the balance sheet has not yet hit the income statement.

The statement of cash flows — indirect method

Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. The statement of cash flows reconciles the change in the cash balance and splits it into three activities. Cash from Operations (CFO) starts from net income and, under the indirect method, adds back non-cash expenses (depreciation), then adjusts for changes in working capital. Cash from Investing (CFI) captures purchases/sales of long-term assets (capital expenditures are negative). Cash from Financing (CFF) captures borrowing, debt repayment, stock issuance, and dividends paid. The three must sum to the change in cash.

Indirect-method working-capital rules (memorize the signs):

  • An increase in a current asset (e.g., receivables, inventory) uses cash ⇒ subtract.
  • A decrease in a current asset provides cash ⇒ add.
  • An increase in a current liability (e.g., payables) provides cash ⇒ add.
  • A decrease in a current liability uses cash ⇒ subtract.

Worked CFO example for MBG: net income $300,000; depreciation $80,000; accounts receivable rose $40,000 (subtract); inventory fell $25,000 (add); accounts payable rose $35,000 (add). CFO = 300,000 + 80,000 − 40,000 + 25,000 + 35,000 = $400,000.

Cash-flow pattern recognition

Exams love asking you to read a company's life stage from the signs of CFO/CFI/CFF. A healthy mature firm shows +CFO, −CFI, −CFF: it generates cash from operations, invests in assets, and returns cash to capital providers (debt repayment, dividends, buybacks). A fast-growing young firm often shows +CFO, −CFI, +CFF: operations are positive but heavy investment is funded by raising new capital. A firm in distress may show −CFO propped up by asset sales (+CFI) and new borrowing (+CFF). Train yourself to translate the three signs into a one-sentence story — that is exactly the conceptual question style.

Ratio analysis and the DuPont identity

Ratios standardize the statements so firms of different sizes are comparable. Four families: liquidity (current ratio = CA/CL; quick ratio = (CA − inventory)/CL), leverage/solvency (debt ratio = total debt/total assets; debt-to-equity = total debt/total equity), profitability (net profit margin = NI/Sales; ROA = NI/Total Assets; ROE = NI/Equity), and efficiency (total asset turnover = Sales/Total Assets; inventory turnover; days sales outstanding).

The DuPont identity decomposes ROE into three levers and is a high-frequency exam item: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier, i.e. (NI/Sales) × (Sales/Total Assets) × (Total Assets/Equity). The terms telescope back to NI/Equity, but the decomposition tells you why ROE is high — fat margins, asset efficiency, or leverage. Worked example for Riverton Development: net profit margin 8%, total asset turnover 1.5, equity multiplier 2.0 ⇒ ROE = 0.08 × 1.5 × 2.0 = 24%. If two firms have the same ROE but one earns it through a 4.0 equity multiplier (heavy debt) and the other through a 12% margin, DuPont exposes the risk difference. Note also ROA = Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover (the first two DuPont terms), and the equity multiplier (Total Assets/Equity) is the bridge from ROA to ROE.

Corporate taxes — marginal vs average

Finance cares about taxes because cash flows are valued after tax. Two rates matter. The marginal tax rate is the rate on the next dollar of income — the rate that matters for any incremental decision (a new project, more debt). The average tax rate is total tax ÷ taxable income — a backward-looking summary. For valuation and capital budgeting you almost always use the marginal rate. Interest is tax-deductible, which is why debt creates a tax shield: a firm paying 25% tax that owes $100,000 of interest saves $25,000 in taxes, lowering the effective cost of debt to rate × (1 − T). This single idea reappears in U2·W3 when we compute the after-tax cost of debt in WACC.

Operating cash flow (finance definition). A common exam figure is OCF = EBIT + Depreciation − Taxes (sometimes written EBIT(1−T) + Depreciation). Depreciation is added back because it is non-cash, yet it lowered taxes — the so-called depreciation tax shield = Depreciation × T. For Northstar: EBIT $2,490,000; depreciation $200,000; taxes $657,000 ⇒ OCF = 2,490,000 + 200,000 − 657,000 = $2,033,000.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: increases in current assets subtract in the indirect CFO build — students reflexively add. Trap 2: DuPont order is margin × turnover × multiplier; don't invert the equity multiplier (it is Total Assets/Equity, always ≥ 1). Trap 3: LIFO gives higher COGS and lower profit when prices rise. Trap 4: use the marginal, not average, tax rate for incremental decisions. Trap 5: retained earnings roll forward — ending RE is not just net income; subtract dividends.

Recap: the income ladder runs Sales → GP → EBIT → EBT → NI → EPS; the balance sheet balances and RE rolls forward; the indirect cash-flow statement splits into CFO/CFI/CFF with strict working-capital signs; DuPont decomposes ROE into margin, turnover, and leverage; and after-tax thinking (marginal rate, interest tax shield) sets up the cost-of-capital work ahead.

weeks.title: Finance U1·W2 — Time Value of Money (PV, FV, Annuities & Perpetuities)
weeks.lessonHtml:
The one idea behind all of finance

A dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow, because today's dollar can be invested to earn a return. Time value of money (TVM) is the machinery for moving cash flows across time so they can be compared on a common date. Almost every later topic — bond pricing, stock valuation, NPV, WACC — is an application of TVM. This week we master the four core relationships and the BA II Plus keystrokes that execute them. The fictional savers and projects here belong to Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Northstar Services.

Future value and present value of a single sum

The two foundational formulas: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n moves money forward; PV = FV / (1 + r)^n moves money back. Here r is the periodic rate and n is the number of periods. Compounding is the forward direction (interest earns interest); discounting is the backward direction. Worked example: MBG invests $10,000 at 6% for 5 years. FV = 10,000 × (1.06)^5 = 10,000 × 1.338226 = $13,382.26. Reverse it: what is $13,382.26 received in 5 years worth today at 6%? PV = 13,382.26 / (1.06)^5 = $10,000. The two operations are perfect inverses.

BA II Plus single-sum keystrokes. Always start with 2ND → CLR TVM. For the FV example: 5 N, 6 I/Y, 10000 +/− PV (cash out is negative), CPT FV → 13,382.26. Note the sign convention: you put $10,000 in (negative) and get a positive FV out. If PV and FV carry the same sign you will get an Error 5.

Solving for rate and time

The same TVM register solves for the unknown rate (I/Y) or number of periods (N). If $8,000 grows to $12,000 over 6 years, the implied annual rate solves 12,000 = 8,000(1+r)^6 ⇒ (1+r)^6 = 1.5 ⇒ r = 1.5^(1/6) − 1 = 6.99%. On the calculator: 2ND CLR TVM, 6 N, 8000 +/− PV, 12000 FV, CPT I/Y → 6.99. To solve for time, enter I/Y and the two dollar amounts and CPT N. These "solve for n or r" problems are common and trivially fast on the BA II Plus once the sign convention is correct.

Annuities — level cash flows over time

An annuity is a stream of equal payments (PMT) at regular intervals. Two formulas, both worth memorizing because conceptual questions ask which factor grows or shrinks:

Present value of an ordinary annuity: PV = PMT × [(1 − (1 + r)^−n) / r]. This values a stream of future payments as of today — the engine behind loan and bond pricing.

Future value of an ordinary annuity: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) / r]. This accumulates a savings stream — the engine behind retirement and sinking-fund problems.

"Ordinary" means payments occur at the end of each period (the BA II Plus default, END mode). Worked PV example: Riverton will receive $2,000 at the end of each year for 10 years; at 8% the present value = 2,000 × [(1 − 1.08^−10)/0.08] = 2,000 × 6.710081 = $13,420.16. Worked FV example: Northstar deposits $3,000 at the end of each year for 20 years at 7%. FV = 3,000 × [(1.07^20 − 1)/0.07] = 3,000 × 40.995492 = $122,986.48.

BA II Plus annuity keystrokes (PV example): 2ND CLR TVM, 10 N, 8 I/Y, 2000 PMT, 0 FV, CPT PV → −13,420.16 (negative because it is the amount you would pay today to receive the stream). Keep PV and PMT on opposite signs.

Perpetuities — payments forever

A perpetuity is an annuity with no end date. Its present value collapses to a remarkably simple formula: PV = PMT / r. Worked example: a fictional endowment pays $5,000 per year forever; if the discount rate is 4%, its value today = 5,000 / 0.04 = $125,000. This is the limiting case of the PV-annuity formula as n → ∞ (the (1+r)^−n term vanishes). The perpetuity formula reappears directly in two later topics: the price of a consol/perpetual bond (Price = Coupon/YTM) and the value of a zero-growth stock or preferred share (P0 = D/r). Recognizing a cash flow as a perpetuity is a major exam shortcut.

A close cousin is the growing perpetuity, a stream that grows at a constant rate g forever, valued as PMT/(r − g). This is the engine of the Gordon stock-valuation model in U2·W1, so it is worth noticing now that a level perpetuity is just a growing perpetuity with g = 0. The structural lesson of this section is that an infinite stream does not require infinite work: whenever payments are level, or grow at a constant rate, and continue forever, a one-line formula replaces an impossible sum, which is exactly why perpetuities anchor both bond and stock valuation later in the course.

The intuition behind the factors

Conceptual questions hinge on knowing the direction each input pushes value. For a present value: a higher discount rate r lowers PV (future money is discounted harder); a longer horizon n lowers PV of a single future sum (more discounting), but raises the PV of an annuity (more payments are received). For a future value: higher r and higher n both raise FV. A useful mental check before any computation: decide whether the answer should be larger or smaller than the cash flow you started with, and confirm the calculator agrees.

Another reliable check is the Rule of 72: money roughly doubles in 72/r years (r in percent). At 8%, doubling takes about 9 years; at 6%, about 12 years. It is an approximation, not an exam answer, but it catches gross keystroke errors instantly — if the calculator says $1,000 grows to $40,000 in 9 years at 8%, the Rule of 72 tells you something is wrong.

Worked multi-step problem

MBG wants $200,000 in 15 years to fund an equipment replacement. It can earn 7% compounded annually. (a) How much must it deposit today as a single sum? PV = 200,000 / 1.07^15 = 200,000 / 2.759032 = $72,489.91. (b) Alternatively, how much must it deposit at the end of each year? Solve the FV-annuity for PMT: 200,000 = PMT × [(1.07^15 − 1)/0.07] = PMT × 25.129022 ⇒ PMT = $7,958.55. On the calculator for (b): 2ND CLR TVM, 15 N, 7 I/Y, 0 PV, 200000 FV, CPT PMT. The two answers describe the same goal funded two different ways — exactly the kind of comparison TVM was built for.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: the periodic rate r and number of periods n must match the payment frequency — if anything is non-annual, convert (covered in detail in U1·W3). Trap 2: ordinary annuity = payments at period end (END mode); leaving BGN mode on after a prior problem silently corrupts the answer. Trap 3: sign convention — PV and PMT/FV on opposite signs, or you get Error 5. Trap 4: a perpetuity is PMT/r, not PMT/(1+r); don't add the extra factor. Trap 5: raising n lowers the PV of a single sum but raises the PV of an annuity — opposite effects, frequently tested.

Recap: FV = PV(1+r)^n and PV = FV/(1+r)^n move single sums across time; the ordinary-annuity PV and FV formulas value and accumulate level streams; the perpetuity collapses to PMT/r; and the BA II Plus TVM register executes all of them once you respect CLR TVM, END mode, and the sign convention.

weeks.title: Finance U1·W3 — Interest Rates, Compounding & Annuities (EAR, Continuous, Annuity Due)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Stated rates lie; effective rates tell the truth

U1·W2 assumed annual compounding. The real world compounds monthly, daily, even continuously, and a quoted ("nominal" or "stated" or APR) rate is not what you actually earn or pay once compounding frequency is layered in. This week makes you fluent in converting between nominal, periodic, and effective rates, in continuous compounding, and in the annuity due / BGN discipline that trips up so many students. Fictional cases use Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Lakeside Retail.

Nominal, periodic, and effective rates

Three rate concepts must be kept distinct. The nominal annual rate (APR) is the quoted rate. The periodic rate is the nominal rate divided by the number of compounding periods per year: periodic = r_nominal / m. The effective annual rate (EAR) is what you truly earn after compounding all m periods: EAR = (1 + r_nominal / m)^m − 1. Worked example: a credit line quotes 12% APR compounded monthly. The periodic rate is 12%/12 = 1% per month, and EAR = (1 + 0.12/12)^12 − 1 = (1.01)^12 − 1 = 12.6825%. The more frequent the compounding, the larger the gap between the nominal rate and the EAR. When comparing two loans or two investments with different compounding frequencies, you must compare EARs, not nominal rates — this is the whole point of the EAR concept.

BA II Plus ICONV worksheet. The calculator converts directly: 2ND → ICONV, enter NOM = 12, C/Y = 12, scroll to EFF, CPT → 12.6825. It also converts the other way (EFF → NOM). For everyday TVM problems, the cleaner discipline is to keep P/Y = C/Y = 1 and feed the calculator the periodic rate and the periodic count directly: for the 12% monthly case over 3 years, use 36 N and 1 I/Y rather than fiddling with P/Y settings — this avoids the most common contamination bug.

Compounding frequency in TVM problems

When a single-sum or annuity problem compounds m times per year, adjust both rate and periods consistently: use periodic rate = nominal/m and number of periods = years × m. Worked example: Lakeside Retail invests $4,000 at 8% compounded quarterly for 5 years. Periodic rate = 8%/4 = 2%; periods = 5 × 4 = 20. FV = 4,000 × (1.02)^20 = 4,000 × 1.485947 = $5,943.79. Compare to annual compounding (FV = 4,000 × 1.08^5 = $5,877.31): quarterly compounding earns more because interest compounds sooner. The lesson: never mix an annual rate with a non-annual period count.

Continuous compounding

As compounding frequency m goes to infinity, the EAR formula converges to the continuous case. The growth factor becomes the exponential: FV = PV × e^(r × t), and the continuous EAR = e^r − 1. Worked example: $10,000 at 6% compounded continuously for 4 years. FV = 10,000 × e^(0.06 × 4) = 10,000 × e^0.24 = 10,000 × 1.271249 = $12,712.49. Continuous EAR at 6% = e^0.06 − 1 = 6.1837%, slightly above the 6% nominal — the theoretical maximum for any compounding frequency at that nominal rate.

BA II Plus continuous keystrokes — and the trap. Do not attempt to fake continuous compounding by setting C/Y to a giant number like 1,000,000; it contaminates the next problem and is a classic error. Instead use the e^x key (2ND → LN): compute the exponent first, then exponentiate, then multiply by PV. For the example: 0.06 × 4 = 0.24, then 2ND LN → 1.271249, then × 10000 = → 12,712.49.

Annuity due — payments at the beginning

An annuity due shifts every payment one period earlier (rent paid at the start of the month, lease payments, some savings plans). Because each cash flow is discounted (or compounded) one period less, an annuity due is always worth (1 + r) times the corresponding ordinary annuity. The formulas: PV(due) = PMT × [(1 − (1+r)^−n)/r] × (1 + r) and FV(due) = PMT × [((1+r)^n − 1)/r] × (1 + r).

Worked example: Riverton pays $1,000 at the beginning of each year for 5 years; at 10%, the ordinary-annuity PV would be 1,000 × 3.790787 = $3,790.79, so the annuity-due PV = 3,790.79 × 1.10 = $4,169.87. The due version is larger because you receive each payment sooner.

BA II Plus BGN discipline — the most-missed setup. To value an annuity due, switch the calculator to begin mode: 2ND → BGN → 2ND → SET (the display shows BGN), then run the TVM keys normally. The non-negotiable rule: turn BGN back OFF after the problem (2ND BGN 2ND SET again until BGN disappears), because a lingering BGN indicator silently corrupts every subsequent ordinary-annuity answer. Before any TVM problem, glance at the screen: if you expect an ordinary annuity and see BGN, clear it. Always pair this with 2ND CLR TVM at the start.

Loan amortization and the AMORT worksheet

A fully amortizing loan is an ordinary annuity from the lender's perspective: the payment is constant, but each payment is part interest and part principal, with the interest portion shrinking over time. To find the payment, treat the loan amount as PV and solve for PMT. Worked example: MBG borrows $50,000 at 9% for 5 annual payments. PV = 50,000, 5 N, 9 I/Y, CPT PMT → $12,854.62. To find the remaining balance after, say, payment 2, use the AMORT worksheet: after solving for PMT, press 2ND → AMORT, set P1 = 1 and P2 = 2, then scroll to BAL to read the outstanding principal. The balance equals the present value of the remaining payments — another TVM application.

Putting it together — comparing offers

Suppose MBG can borrow at 11.8% compounded daily or 12.0% compounded annually. Which is cheaper? Convert both to EAR. The 11.8% daily: EAR = (1 + 0.118/365)^365 − 1 ≈ 12.52%. The 12.0% annual is, by definition, EAR = 12.0%. Despite the lower nominal rate, the daily-compounded loan is more expensive once compounding is accounted for. This is precisely why regulators force lenders to disclose an effective figure, and why the exam insists you compare on an EAR basis whenever frequencies differ.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: comparing two rates with different compounding frequencies by their nominal rates — always convert to EAR. Trap 2: mixing an annual rate with a non-annual period count (use periodic rate with periodic n). Trap 3: faking continuous compounding with a huge C/Y — use the e^x key instead. Trap 4: leaving BGN mode on after an annuity-due problem, which silently corrupts the next ordinary annuity — always reset and verify the indicator. Trap 5: an annuity due equals the ordinary annuity × (1 + r); don't forget the extra factor, and don't apply it twice.

Recap: EAR = (1 + r/m)^m − 1 reconciles nominal and effective rates; quarterly/monthly TVM uses periodic rate and periodic n; continuous compounding uses FV = PV·e^(r·t) and EAR = e^r − 1; an annuity due is worth (1 + r) times the ordinary annuity and requires BGN mode (reset afterward); and the AMORT worksheet reads any remaining loan balance.

weeks.title: Finance U1·W4 — Bonds & Bond Valuation
weeks.lessonHtml:
A bond is just a TVM problem with a name

A bond is a loan packaged as a tradable security. The issuer promises (1) periodic coupon payments and (2) repayment of par/face value at maturity. Its price is nothing more than the present value of those cash flows discounted at the market's required rate — the yield to maturity (YTM). Everything this week is an application of the annuity-plus-lump-sum machinery from U1·W2–W3, but bonds are a heavily tested, frequently missed topic, so we go deep with worked examples, the semiannual setup, and the price–yield relationships. Fictional issuers: Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Keystone Freight.

The five bond inputs and the pricing identity

Every bond price is built from five inputs that map exactly onto the BA II Plus TVM keys: N = number of periods to maturity; I/Y = required return (YTM) per period; PMT = coupon per period; FV = par (usually $1,000); solve CPT PV = price. Conceptually, Price = PV(coupon annuity) + PV(par lump sum): Price = Coupon × [(1 − (1+r)^−N)/r] + Par/(1+r)^N. The coupon rate (a fixed contractual percentage of par) determines the dollar coupon and never changes; the YTM is set by the market and moves daily, which is why bond prices move even though coupons are fixed.

The semiannual setup — the #1 exam trap

US bonds almost always pay coupons twice a year, and the single most common bond error is forgetting to convert every input to a semiannual basis. The conversions, memorize them cold:

  • N = years × 2 (number of semiannual periods)
  • I/Y = annual YTM ÷ 2 (semiannual yield)
  • PMT = annual coupon ÷ 2 (semiannual coupon dollars)
  • FV = par (unchanged — still $1,000 at maturity)

Worked example: MBG issues a 10-year bond, 8% annual coupon, par $1,000, with the market demanding a 6% YTM, paid semiannually. Convert: N = 20, I/Y = 3, PMT = 40, FV = 1,000. Keystrokes: 2ND CLR TVM, 20 N, 3 I/Y, 40 PMT, 1000 FV, CPT PV → −$1,148.77. The price is $1,148.77 (the negative sign is just the calculator's cash-out convention). Because the 8% coupon exceeds the 6% yield, the bond trades at a premium — more on that next.

Premium, discount, and par — by inspection

You can state whether a bond trades above or below par before computing anything, just by comparing the coupon rate to the YTM:

  • Coupon rate > YTM ⇒ PREMIUM (price > par). The bond pays more than the market demands, so buyers bid the price up.
  • Coupon rate < YTM ⇒ DISCOUNT (price < par). The bond pays less than the market demands, so the price falls until the effective yield matches.
  • Coupon rate = YTM ⇒ PAR (price = par). The cash flows exactly satisfy the required return.

Use this as a built-in check: if you compute a price below par for a bond whose coupon exceeds its yield, you made a keystroke error. Worked discount example: Riverton's 5-year, 4% annual-coupon bond (semiannual) when the market yield is 6%. N = 10, I/Y = 3, PMT = 20, FV = 1,000 ⇒ Price = $914.70 — below par, exactly as the coupon < YTM rule predicts.

Yield to maturity — solving the inverse problem

YTM is the discount rate that makes the present value of the bond's cash flows equal its market price — the bond's internal rate of return if held to maturity. You cannot solve it algebraically; you let the calculator iterate. Given the price, enter N, PMT, FV, and the price as PV (opposite sign to FV/PMT), then CPT I/Y. Worked example: Keystone Freight's 8-year bond, 7% annual coupon, semiannual, currently priced at $1,050. Convert: N = 16, PMT = 35, FV = 1,000, PV = −1,050. CPT I/Y → 3.1156% per period; the annual YTM = 3.1156% × 2 = 6.23%. Note YTM < coupon (7%), consistent with the premium price. Don't forget to double the calculator's periodic I/Y to report the annual (bond-equivalent) yield — another classic miss.

Zero-coupon bonds

A zero-coupon bond pays no coupons; it is bought at a deep discount and redeemed at par, so its price is a single discounted lump sum: Price = Par / (1 + r)^n. If a problem specifies semiannual compounding conventions, use r = YTM/2 and n = years × 2. Worked example: a fictional 12-year zero, par $1,000, priced to yield 5% with semiannual compounding. n = 24, r = 2.5%. Price = 1,000 / 1.025^24 = 1,000 / 1.808726 = $552.88. Zeros are the workhorse of interest-rate-sensitivity questions because all of their value sits at maturity.

Consols and perpetual bonds

A consol (perpetual bond) pays a fixed coupon forever with no maturity. It is simply a perpetuity, so Price = Coupon / YTM. Worked example: a perpetual bond paying $60 per year when the required yield is 5% is worth 60 / 0.05 = $1,200. This is the same PMT/r perpetuity formula from U1·W2, reused — recognizing the pattern earns easy points.

Interest-rate sensitivity — the relationships to memorize

Bond prices and market yields move in opposite directions: when required yields rise, the present value of fixed future cash flows falls, so prices drop, and vice versa. The magnitude of that price move depends on three features:

  1. Maturity: longer-maturity bonds are MORE sensitive (more cash flows are discounted, and the big par repayment is pushed further out).
  2. Coupon: lower-coupon bonds are MORE sensitive (a larger share of value sits in the distant par payment).
  3. Zero-coupon bonds are the MOST sensitive of all — they combine the longest effective timing with the lowest possible coupon (zero).

So if an exam asks which of several bonds will fall most when rates rise, pick the longest-maturity, lowest-coupon (ideally zero-coupon) bond. The intuition: sensitivity is about how far out in time the cash flows sit, and zeros put 100% of their value at the final date.

Current yield vs YTM

Two yield measures are often confused. Current yield = annual coupon / current price — a simple income measure that ignores the gain or loss from price converging to par. YTM is the total return including that convergence. For a premium bond, price drifts down toward par over time, so YTM < current yield < coupon rate. For a discount bond, price drifts up toward par, so YTM > current yield > coupon rate. At par all three are equal. Knowing this ordering is a frequent conceptual question.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: forgetting the semiannual conversion — N = yrs×2, I/Y = rate/2, PMT = coupon/2, FV = par. Trap 2: reporting the periodic I/Y from CPT without doubling it to get the annual YTM. Trap 3: mis-signing — PV must be opposite in sign to PMT and FV, or Error 5. Trap 4: ignoring the premium/discount sanity check (coupon vs YTM). Trap 5: picking the short-maturity, high-coupon bond as "most sensitive" — it's the opposite; zero-coupon and long maturity are most sensitive.

Recap: a bond price is PV(coupons) + PV(par) at the YTM; semiannual bonds need all four inputs converted; coupon vs YTM tells you premium/discount/par instantly; zeros price as Par/(1+r)^n and consols as Coupon/YTM; prices move inversely to yields, and long-maturity, low-coupon, zero-coupon bonds are the most rate-sensitive.

flashcards.back: Price = Coupon × [(1 − (1+r)^−N)/r] + Par/(1+r)^N = PV(coupons) + PV(par).

weeks.title: Finance U2·W1 — Stocks & Dividend Growth (the Gordon Model)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Valuing a share as a stream of dividends

A share of common stock is a claim on a company's future dividends. Its intrinsic value is the present value of all expected future dividends discounted at the investor's required return. Because dividends extend forever and (for most firms) grow over time, we use a perpetuity-with-growth shortcut: the constant-growth dividend discount model, universally called the Gordon Growth Model (DGM). This week makes you fluent in the Gordon formula, its rearrangements, and the one trap that costs students the most points — the D0-versus-D1 distinction. Fictional companies: Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Northstar Services.

The Gordon Growth Model

If dividends grow at a constant rate g forever and the required return is r (with r > g), the price today is: P0 = D1 / (r − g), where D1 is the dividend expected one period from now. Equivalently, since D1 = D0(1 + g), the model can be written P0 = D0(1 + g) / (r − g). The (r − g) denominator is the "net" discount rate after crediting growth; it must be positive, which is why the model requires r > g (a perpetually higher growth than discount rate would imply infinite value and is economically impossible long-run).

Worked example: Riverton just established a policy and will pay D1 = $2.00 next year, growing 4% forever, with investors requiring 10%. P0 = 2.00 / (0.10 − 0.04) = 2.00 / 0.06 = $33.33. Notice the model is the perpetuity formula PMT/r from U1·W2, generalized to a growing payment.

The D0 vs D1 trap — the single biggest miss

The Gordon formula needs D1, the NEXT dividend. Problems frequently quote the dividend that was just paid, which is D0. If a problem says "the company just paid a dividend of $3.00" or "the most recent dividend was $3.00," that is D0, and you must grow it one period first: D1 = D0 × (1 + g) before plugging into the model. Plugging D0 straight into P0 = D/(r − g) understates the price and is the classic error.

Worked example: Northstar just paid a $3.00 dividend (so D0 = $3.00), g = 5%, r = 12%. First compute D1 = 3.00 × 1.05 = $3.15. Then P0 = 3.15 / (0.12 − 0.05) = 3.15 / 0.07 = $45.00. If you had wrongly used D0 = $3.00 you would get $42.86 — a wrong answer engineered into the choices. The discipline: read carefully for "just paid" / "most recent" (⇒ D0, multiply by 1+g) versus "expected next year" / "will pay" (⇒ already D1, use directly).

Solving for the required return r

Rearranging Gordon gives the investor's expected/required return from a known price: r = D1/P0 + g. The two pieces have names worth knowing: D1/P0 is the dividend yield and g is the capital gains yield (the price of a constant-growth stock grows at g). So total return = dividend yield + capital gains yield. Worked example: MBG stock trades at $40, will pay D1 = $2.40 next year, and dividends grow 6%. r = 2.40/40 + 0.06 = 0.06 + 0.06 = 12%. This rearrangement is also exactly how we will estimate the cost of equity via the DGM in U2·W3 — the same equation, used to find r instead of P0.

Zero-growth stock and preferred stock

When g = 0 (a stock or, classically, a preferred share paying a fixed dividend forever), Gordon collapses to the plain perpetuity: P0 = D / r. Worked example: a fictional preferred share pays a fixed $5.00 dividend with a required return of 8%. P0 = 5.00 / 0.08 = $62.50. Because preferred dividends are fixed, D0 = D1 = D and there is no growth adjustment — a small simplification that occasionally appears as its own question.

Comparative statics — how the inputs move price

Conceptual questions ask which way price moves when an input changes. From P0 = D1/(r − g):

  • D1 up ⇒ P0 up (larger numerator).
  • g up ⇒ P0 up (smaller denominator, and a larger D1) — strongly positive, because g appears twice.
  • r up ⇒ P0 down (larger denominator). A higher required return — from higher risk or higher market rates — lowers the value of the same dividend stream.

The g effect is the most powerful because it both raises the expected dividend and shrinks the (r − g) denominator, which is why small changes in the assumed growth rate cause large swings in DGM valuations — a known sensitivity and a frequent exam talking point. As g approaches r, the denominator approaches zero and the price explodes toward infinity, illustrating why the model is only valid for stable, mature firms where r comfortably exceeds g.

Multi-stage intuition and model limits

The constant-growth model assumes a single growth rate forever. Real high-growth firms grow fast for a few years, then settle to a sustainable long-run rate. The exam-level approach (a two-stage model) discounts the explicit near-term dividends individually, then applies Gordon at the transition year to capture the stable-growth tail (a terminal value), and discounts that back. While full multi-stage problems are heavier, the key insight is reusable: any constant-growth perpetuity that starts in year t has a value at year t−1 of D_t/(r − g), which you then discount to today. Recognizing where to graft a Gordon terminal value onto an explicit forecast is the bridge from this week's single-stage model to richer valuations.

The model's limits are also testable: it cannot value a firm that pays no dividends and has no foreseeable dividend, it is invalid when g ≥ r, and it is hypersensitive to the g and r assumptions. These limitations are why analysts cross-check the DGM against multiples and discounted-cash-flow models — but for the exam, the single-stage Gordon model, applied with correct D0/D1 discipline, handles the large majority of stock-valuation questions.

Worked synthesis problem

MBG just paid an annual dividend of $1.80 (so D0 = $1.80). Analysts expect 7% constant growth and investors require a 13% return. (a) Price today: D1 = 1.80 × 1.07 = $1.926; P0 = 1.926 / (0.13 − 0.07) = 1.926 / 0.06 = $32.10. (b) Expected price in one year: a constant-growth stock grows at g, so P1 = P0 × (1 + g) = 32.10 × 1.07 = $34.35 (equivalently P1 = D2/(r − g) with D2 = 1.926 × 1.07). (c) Decompose this year's expected return: dividend yield = D1/P0 = 1.926/32.10 = 6%; capital gains yield = g = 7%? — recheck: total must equal r = 13%, so capital gains yield = 7% and dividend yield = 6%, summing to 13%. The pieces reconcile, confirming the arithmetic.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: using a "just paid" dividend as D1 — it is D0; multiply by (1 + g) first. Trap 2: forgetting the model needs r > g; if not, the formula is invalid. Trap 3: in r = D1/P0 + g, using D0 instead of D1 in the dividend-yield term. Trap 4: treating g as affecting only the denominator — it raises D1 too. Trap 5: for preferred/zero-growth stock, don't apply a growth factor; P0 = D/r.

Recap: P0 = D1/(r − g) = D0(1+g)/(r − g); D0 is "just paid" and must be grown to D1; r = D1/P0 + g splits total return into dividend yield plus capital-gains yield (g); zero-growth/preferred stock is P0 = D/r; and price rises with D1 and g, falls with r, with g the most powerful lever.

flashcards.back: P0 = D1 / (r − g) = D0(1 + g) / (r − g), valid only when r > g.
D0 = dividend just paid (most recent); D1 = next expected dividend = D0(1 + g). Gordon needs D1.

weeks.title: Finance U2·W2 — Risk, Return & CAPM
weeks.lessonHtml:
Return is the reward; risk is what you pay for it

Investors demand higher expected returns to bear higher risk. This week quantifies both sides — average return, variance, and standard deviation on the risk side; the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and beta on the pricing side — and nails the two statistics traps that recur on exams: using the population (n) standard-deviation formula, and not subtracting the risk-free rate twice when the market risk premium is already given. Fictional securities belong to Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Northstar Services.

Expected and average return

The average (mean) return over a set of historical periods is simply Average = ΣRi / n. The expected return from a probability distribution weights each possible return by its probability: E(R) = Σ pi × Ri. Worked example (historical): Riverton's annual returns over four years were 10%, −4%, 16%, and 6%. Average = (10 − 4 + 16 + 6)/4 = 28/4 = 7%. Worked example (probabilistic): a stock returns 20% with probability 0.3, 8% with probability 0.5, and −5% with probability 0.2. E(R) = 0.3(20) + 0.5(8) + 0.2(−5) = 6 + 4 − 1 = 9%. Get the mean right first — every dispersion measure is built around it.

Variance and standard deviation — use population n

Standard deviation measures total risk (dispersion of returns around the mean). The population variance divides by n: σ² = Σ(Ri − μ)² / n, and σ = √(σ²). This course's convention — and the high-yield trap — is to use n, the population formula, NOT n − 1 (the sample formula). When a problem hands you the complete set of outcomes (treat it as the entire population), divide by n. Using n − 1 inflates the denominator's correction and produces a wrong, slightly larger σ — the single most common dispersion error.

Worked example: Riverton's four returns (10%, −4%, 16%, 6%) have mean 7%. Deviations: +3, −11, +9, −1; squared: 9, 121, 81, 1; sum = 212. Population variance = 212/4 = 53 (in percent-squared); σ = √53 = 7.28%. (If you wrongly used n − 1 = 3 you'd get √(212/3) = 8.40% — the trap answer.) On the BA II Plus you can use the statistics worksheet, but the formula is fast enough by hand for four data points, and doing it by hand guarantees you control the n-vs-(n−1) choice.

Systematic vs unsystematic risk and beta

Total risk splits into two parts. Unsystematic (diversifiable) risk is firm-specific — a lawsuit, a failed product, a key-person loss — and it can be eliminated by holding a diversified portfolio. Systematic (market) risk is economy-wide — interest rates, recessions, inflation — and cannot be diversified away. Because investors can shed unsystematic risk for free through diversification, the market only rewards systematic risk. Beta (β) measures a security's systematic risk relative to the overall market: the market has β = 1.0; a stock with β = 1.5 moves 1.5× the market (more systematic risk, higher required return); a stock with β = 0.6 is defensive; β = 0 is risk-free in the systematic sense. This is the conceptual foundation for CAPM: required return should depend on β, not on total standard deviation.

CAPM and the Security Market Line

The Capital Asset Pricing Model prices systematic risk: Required Return = Rf + β(Rm − Rf), where Rf is the risk-free rate, Rm is the expected market return, and (Rm − Rf) is the market risk premium — the extra return investors demand for bearing one unit of market risk. Plotting required return against β gives the Security Market Line (SML): it starts at Rf (where β = 0) and rises with slope equal to the market risk premium. Any correctly priced security lies on the SML.

Worked example: Rf = 3%, expected market return Rm = 9%, MBG's β = 1.2. Required return = 3% + 1.2 × (9% − 3%) = 3% + 1.2 × 6% = 3% + 7.2% = 10.2%. The market risk premium here is 6%; MBG, being more volatile than the market (β > 1), earns a premium above the market's 9% would not be right — actually below or above depends on β: at β = 1.2 the required return 10.2% exceeds the market's 9%, consistent with higher-than-market systematic risk.

The market-risk-premium trap — don't subtract Rf twice

The most punishing CAPM trap: some problems give you the market risk premium (Rm − Rf) directly rather than the market return Rm. In that case the bracket is already (Rm − Rf) — you multiply it by β and add Rf once; you must not subtract Rf again. Worked example: Rf = 4%, the market risk premium is given as 5%, β = 1.3. Required return = 4% + 1.3 × 5% = 4% + 6.5% = 10.5%. The wrong move is to treat the 5% as Rm and compute 4% + 1.3(5% − 4%) = 5.3%, which mis-reads a premium as a return. Read the problem precisely: "expected market return" ⇒ subtract Rf inside the bracket; "market risk premium" (or "equity risk premium") ⇒ it is already the bracket, use it as is.

Portfolio return and portfolio beta

A portfolio's expected return is the weighted average of its holdings' expected returns: E(Rp) = Σ wi × E(Ri), where wi are the value weights. Likewise, a portfolio's beta is the weighted average of the component betas: βp = Σ wi × βi. Worked example: a portfolio holds 60% MBG (E(R) = 12%, β = 1.4) and 40% Northstar (E(R) = 7%, β = 0.8). E(Rp) = 0.6(12) + 0.4(7) = 7.2 + 2.8 = 10%; βp = 0.6(1.4) + 0.4(0.8) = 0.84 + 0.32 = 1.16. Note that while expected returns and betas average linearly, portfolio standard deviation does NOT — diversification means σp is generally less than the weighted average of the individual σ's whenever the assets are not perfectly correlated. That gap is the entire benefit of diversification.

Using CAPM to judge a security

CAPM gives a benchmark required return; comparing it to a security's expected return tells you whether the security is attractive. If expected return > CAPM required return, the security plots above the SML and is underpriced (a buy); if expected return < required return, it plots below the SML and is overpriced. Worked example: Riverton has β = 1.0 with Rf = 3% and market risk premium 6%, so CAPM required return = 3% + 1.0(6%) = 9%. If analysts expect Riverton to actually return 11%, it offers 2% more than its risk warrants — underpriced, above the SML. This SML-positioning logic is a favorite conceptual question and connects directly to the cost of equity used in WACC next week.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: standard deviation uses n (population), not n − 1 — divide by the count of outcomes. Trap 2: if the market risk premium is given, the bracket is already (Rm − Rf); multiply by β and add Rf once — do not subtract Rf again. Trap 3: only systematic risk (β) is rewarded; total σ and unsystematic risk are not priced by CAPM. Trap 4: portfolio σ is NOT the weighted average of individual σ's (returns and betas are; standard deviation isn't). Trap 5: compute the mean before any deviation — an error in μ propagates into every squared term.

Recap: average = ΣRi/n and expected return = Σpi·Ri; population σ divides squared deviations by n; beta measures systematic (non-diversifiable) risk; CAPM = Rf + β(Rm − Rf) is the SML; when the premium (Rm − Rf) is given, use it directly; and portfolio return and beta are weighted averages while portfolio standard deviation benefits from diversification.

flashcards.back: Average (historical) = ΣRi / n. Expected (probabilistic) = Σ pi × Ri.
σ = √(Σ(Ri − μ)² / n). Use n (POPULATION), NOT n − 1, when given the full set of outcomes.
Systematic (market) risk can't be diversified and IS rewarded; unsystematic (firm-specific) risk is diversifiable and NOT rewarded.
Measures systematic risk vs the market (market β = 1). β > 1 = more volatile; β < 1 = defensive.
Required Return = Rf + β(Rm − Rf); (Rm − Rf) is the market risk premium.
If (Rm − Rf) is GIVEN, multiply by β and add Rf ONCE; do not subtract Rf again.
Both are weighted averages: E(Rp) = Σ wi·E(Ri); βp = Σ wi·βi.

flashcards.front: Why isn't portfolio σ a weighted average?
flashcards.back: Diversification: unless assets are perfectly correlated, σp is LESS than the weighted average of individual σ's.

weeks.title: Finance U2·W3 — Cost of Capital / WACC
weeks.lessonHtml:
The hurdle rate every project must clear

A firm raises money from two broad sources — debt and equity — and each has a cost. The blended cost, weighted by how much of each the firm uses, is the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). WACC is the discount rate used in capital budgeting (next week) and the threshold a new investment must beat to create value. This week assembles WACC from its parts: the after-tax cost of debt, the cost of equity (via CAPM and via the dividend model), the cost of preferred stock, and the capital-structure weights. Fictional firms: Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Northstar Services.

The WACC formula

For a firm financed with debt and common equity (and optionally preferred stock): WACC = wd × rd × (1 − T) + wp × rp + we × re, where the w's are the proportions of each source in the capital structure (they sum to 1), rd is the pre-tax cost of debt, rp the cost of preferred, re the cost of equity, and T the marginal tax rate. The (1 − T) factor appears only on debt because interest is tax-deductible — debt enjoys a tax shield that equity and preferred do not. With debt and equity only, this reduces to WACC = wd × rd × (1 − T) + we × re.

Cost of debt — pre-tax and after-tax

The pre-tax cost of debt (rd) is the yield the firm must currently pay to borrow — effectively the YTM on its outstanding bonds (from U1·W4), not the historical coupon. Because interest is deductible, what matters for WACC is the after-tax cost of debt = rd × (1 − T). Worked example: MBG's bonds yield 7% and its marginal tax rate is 25%. After-tax cost of debt = 7% × (1 − 0.25) = 7% × 0.75 = 5.25%. The tax shield knocks 1.75 percentage points off the cost — the practical reason firms value debt financing, and the link back to the interest tax shield introduced in U1·W1.

Cost of equity — two routes

Equity has no contractual rate, so we estimate it. Two methods, both worth knowing because problems specify which to use:

Method 1 — CAPM: re = Rf + β(Rm − Rf), exactly the CAPM from U2·W2. Worked example: Rf = 3%, market risk premium 6%, MBG's β = 1.2 ⇒ re = 3% + 1.2(6%) = 10.2%. (Remember the trap: if the premium is given, don't subtract Rf again.)

Method 2 — Dividend Growth Model: rearranging Gordon from U2·W1, re = D1/P0 + g (dividend yield plus growth). Worked example: Riverton's stock is $40, D1 = $2.40, g = 6% ⇒ re = 2.40/40 + 0.06 = 6% + 6% = 12%. When a problem gives both a beta and a dividend stream, it usually wants one specific method — read carefully; sometimes the two are averaged. Some problems add a flotation cost adjustment for newly issued equity, raising re because issuance fees reduce net proceeds; the exam-level treatment divides D1 by the net price (P0 − flotation) in the DGM.

Cost of preferred stock

Preferred stock pays a fixed dividend forever, so its cost is the zero-growth perpetuity rearranged: rp = Dp / Pp, where Dp is the annual preferred dividend and Pp the preferred price. No tax adjustment — preferred dividends are not tax-deductible. Worked example: a fictional preferred share pays $5.00 and trades at $50 ⇒ rp = 5.00/50 = 10%. Preferred sits between debt and common equity in the cost ranking: riskier (and costlier) than debt because it lacks the tax shield and is junior, but cheaper than common equity because its dividend is fixed and it has priority over common.

Capital-structure weights — use market values

The weights should reflect market values of each financing source, not book values, because WACC is a forward-looking rate for raising new capital at current prices. Compute the market value of debt (price × bonds), preferred (price × shares), and equity (price × shares), sum to total firm value, and divide each component by the total. Worked example: MBG has equity worth $60 million and debt worth $40 million, so total = $100 million; we = 0.60, wd = 0.40. A frequent error is using the book value of equity (which can differ wildly from market cap) — for the cost of new capital, market values are correct.

Assembling the full WACC

Worked synthesis for MBG: weights we = 0.60, wd = 0.40; cost of equity re = 10.2% (CAPM above); pre-tax cost of debt rd = 7%; tax rate T = 25%. WACC = wd × rd × (1 − T) + we × re = 0.40 × 7% × 0.75 + 0.60 × 10.2% = 0.40 × 5.25% + 6.12% = 2.10% + 6.12% = 8.22%. This 8.22% becomes the discount rate MBG applies to average-risk projects in capital budgeting. Two disciplines to keep straight: apply the (1 − T) factor only to debt, and make sure your weights sum to exactly 1 before combining.

What WACC is — and is not — used for

WACC is the correct hurdle rate only for projects of average risk — projects that resemble the firm's existing business. Using the company-wide WACC to evaluate a project that is much riskier (or safer) than the firm overall is a conceptual error the exam tests: a low-risk project judged against a high WACC may be wrongly rejected, and a high-risk project judged against a low WACC may be wrongly accepted. The fix is a project-specific or divisional discount rate that reflects the project's own systematic risk (its own beta). Also note WACC uses the marginal tax rate and current market costs — it is a rate for the next dollar of capital, not an average of historically issued securities.

Two comparative-statics points are testable. First, all else equal, adding more debt initially lowers WACC (debt is cheaper and tax-advantaged), but beyond a point rising financial risk pushes up both rd and re, so WACC eventually rises — giving the U-shaped WACC curve and an optimal capital structure. Second, a higher tax rate lowers the after-tax cost of debt and therefore lowers WACC, holding weights fixed — a direct consequence of the larger interest tax shield.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: applying the (1 − T) tax shield to equity or preferred — it belongs to debt only. Trap 2: using the coupon rate instead of the current YTM for the cost of debt. Trap 3: using book-value weights instead of market-value weights. Trap 4: using the firm-wide WACC for an off-risk project. Trap 5: in the DGM cost of equity, using D0 instead of D1 (grow a "just paid" dividend first), the same trap as U2·W1.

Recap: WACC = wd·rd(1−T) + wp·rp + we·re; after-tax cost of debt = rd(1−T) using the current YTM; cost of equity via CAPM (Rf + β(Rm−Rf)) or DGM (D1/P0 + g); cost of preferred = Dp/Pp with no tax shield; weights use market values; and WACC is the hurdle rate for average-risk projects only.

weeks.title: Finance U2·W4 — Capital Budgeting (NPV, IRR, Payback, PI & EAA)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Deciding which projects create value

Capital budgeting is how a firm chooses which long-term investments to make. Each candidate project is a stream of cash flows — an upfront cost followed by future inflows — and the question is whether those inflows, discounted at the firm's cost of capital (the WACC from U2·W3), are worth more than the cost. This week covers the five standard rules — NPV, IRR, payback, the profitability index, and equivalent annual annuity — when they agree, when they conflict, and why NPV is the rule that is always right. Fictional projects belong to Meridian Building Group (MBG), Riverton Development, and Northstar Services.

Net present value — the gold standard

NPV is the present value of all future cash flows minus the initial cost: NPV = Σ[CFt / (1 + r)^t] − Initial Cost, where r is the discount rate (cost of capital). The decision rule is simple: accept if NPV > 0 (the project adds value), reject if NPV < 0. NPV measures the dollar increase in firm value, which is exactly the objective of corporate finance, so it is the benchmark against which the other rules are judged.

Worked example: MBG considers a project costing $100,000 that returns $40,000, $50,000, and $30,000 over three years, discounted at 10%. PV of inflows = 40,000/1.10 + 50,000/1.10² + 30,000/1.10³ = 36,363.64 + 41,322.31 + 22,539.44 = 100,225.39. NPV = 100,225.39 − 100,000 = $225.39 > 0 ⇒ accept (barely). BA II Plus: CF → 2ND CLR WORK, CF0 = −100000, C01 = 40000, C02 = 50000, C03 = 30000, then NPV, I = 10, CPT → 225.39. Always use the CF worksheet rather than discounting each term separately — it avoids the rounding drift that produces near-miss wrong answers.

Internal rate of return

The IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV exactly zero — the project's own compound rate of return. The rule: accept if IRR > cost of capital. It cannot be solved algebraically; the calculator iterates: after entering the cash flows, press IRR → CPT. For the MBG project above, IRR ≈ 10.16%, which exceeds the 10% cost of capital — the same accept decision NPV gave (consistent because NPV > 0 ⇔ IRR > r for a normal project). The crucial conceptual point: IRR depends only on the project's cash flows, so changing the cost of capital does NOT change the IRR — it only changes whether the IRR clears the hurdle.

Payback and discounted payback

The payback period is the time until cumulative cash inflows recover the initial cost. Worked example: a $90,000 project returns $30,000, $40,000, then $50,000. After year 1: $30,000; after year 2: $70,000; it needs $20,000 more of the year-3 $50,000, so payback = 2 + 20,000/50,000 = 2.4 years. Payback is intuitive and measures liquidity, but it has two fatal flaws: it ignores the time value of money and it ignores all cash flows after the cutoff. The discounted payback fixes the first flaw by recovering the cost from discounted cash flows, but still ignores everything past the cutoff. Neither is a value-maximizing rule; they are screening/secondary tools.

Profitability index

The profitability index (PI) scales value created per dollar invested: PI = PV of future cash flows / Initial Cost. The rule: accept if PI > 1.0 (which is exactly equivalent to NPV > 0, since PI > 1 means PV of inflows exceeds cost). Worked example: the MBG project's PV of inflows was $100,225.39 on a $100,000 cost, so PI = 100,225.39/100,000 = 1.0023 > 1 ⇒ accept. PI is most useful for capital rationing — when a limited budget forces you to rank projects, PI ranks by bang-per-buck. Note the equivalences: PI > 1 ⇔ NPV > 0 ⇔ IRR > r; PI < 1 ⇔ NPV < 0 ⇔ reject.

Key relationships to memorize

  1. Cost of capital ↓ ⇒ NPV ↑. A lower discount rate makes future cash flows worth more today, raising NPV. (And vice versa: a higher discount rate lowers NPV.)
  2. A change in the cost of capital has NO effect on IRR. IRR is computed purely from the cash flows; the discount rate only sets the hurdle the IRR is compared against.
  3. Later cash flows are MORE sensitive to the discount rate than near-term cash flows (they are discounted over more periods), so projects whose payoffs are back-loaded see NPV swing the most when r changes.
  4. PI < 1.0 ⇒ NPV is negative ⇒ reject.
  5. NPV is the only rule that always gives the value-maximizing answer. When rules conflict, follow NPV.

When NPV and IRR conflict

For a single, independent, conventional project, NPV and IRR always agree. They can conflict for mutually exclusive projects (you can pick only one) that differ in scale or cash-flow timing. IRR is a percentage and ignores project size, so it may favor a small high-percentage project over a larger project that creates more total dollar value. Because the goal is to maximize firm value in dollars, choose the higher-NPV project when they disagree. IRR also has technical problems: non-conventional cash flows (sign changes more than once) can produce multiple IRRs or none, and IRR implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR rather than at the cost of capital. These are the reasons NPV is the theoretically dominant rule, a heavily tested conceptual point.

Equivalent annual annuity — comparing unequal lives

When mutually exclusive projects have different lifespans, comparing raw NPVs is unfair — a longer project has more years to accumulate value. The equivalent annual annuity (EAA) converts each project's NPV into a level annual cash flow over its own life, so they can be compared on a per-year basis: EAA = NPV / annuity factor, where the annuity factor = [(1 − (1+r)^−n)/r] for that project's life n at rate r. Choose the project with the higher EAA. Worked example: Project A has NPV $10,000 over 3 years; Project B has NPV $13,000 over 5 years; r = 8%. A's 3-year annuity factor = 2.577097, so EAA(A) = 10,000/2.577097 = $3,880.34/yr. B's 5-year factor = 3.992710, so EAA(B) = 13,000/3.992710 = $3,255.92/yr. Despite B's higher total NPV, A has the higher EAA and is preferred on a comparable annual basis (assuming the projects can be repeated). EAA is the clean way to handle the unequal-life trap.

Worked synthesis problem

Northstar evaluates a project: cost $200,000; cash flows $80,000, $90,000, $70,000, $60,000 over four years; cost of capital 12%. (a) NPV: PV = 80,000/1.12 + 90,000/1.12² + 70,000/1.12³ + 60,000/1.12⁴ = 71,428.57 + 71,747.45 + 49,824.62 + 38,131.08 = 231,131.72; NPV = 231,131.72 − 200,000 = $31,131.72 ⇒ accept. (b) PI = 231,131.72/200,000 = 1.156 > 1 ⇒ accept (consistent). (c) Payback: after year 1 $80,000; year 2 $170,000; needs $30,000 of year-3's $70,000 ⇒ 2 + 30,000/70,000 = 2.43 years. All three rules agree, as they must for a single conventional project with positive NPV.

Exam traps and recap

Trap 1: believing the cost of capital changes the IRR — it does not; IRR is from cash flows only. Trap 2: choosing the higher-IRR project among mutually exclusive options — pick higher NPV when they conflict. Trap 3: trusting payback as a value rule — it ignores time value and post-cutoff cash flows. Trap 4: comparing unequal-life projects by raw NPV — convert to EAA. Trap 5: discounting each cash flow by hand instead of using the CF worksheet, inviting rounding error; and forgetting CF0 is negative (the cost).

Recap: NPV = Σ CFt/(1+r)^t − Cost (accept if > 0) is the value-maximizing rule; IRR sets NPV = 0 (accept if > r) and is unaffected by the cost of capital; PI = PV inflows/Cost (accept if > 1) ranks under rationing; payback ignores time value and later cash flows; EAA compares unequal lives; and when rules conflict, NPV wins.

weeks.title: Finance U3·W1 — Project Cash Flows & Incremental Analysis
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — which cash flows actually count

Capital budgeting (Unit 2) gave us NPV and IRR; this week supplies the cash flows those tools discount. The single most-tested skill is deciding which cash flows belong in a project decision and when. The rule is unforgiving: only incremental, after-tax cash flows — future amounts that change because the project is accepted — matter. Get the cash flows right and the NPV follows; get them wrong and the most elegant discounting is worthless. A fictional firm, Northstar Services, anchors the examples.

The relevant-cash-flow principle

A cash flow is relevant only if it is incremental — it occurs because of the project and would not occur otherwise. Three corollaries follow. Sunk costs (money already spent, like a completed feasibility study) are ignored. Opportunity costs (the value of a resource's best alternative use, such as a building the firm could have rented out) are included. And side effects — erosion/cannibalization of existing sales, or complementary synergies — are included to the extent they change firm-wide cash flow. Allocated overhead is relevant only if it actually increases because of the project.

The three cash-flow stages

Project cash flows fall into three stages. The initial outlay (time 0) is the cost of the asset plus installation and shipping, plus the initial investment in net working capital, less any after-tax proceeds from an asset being replaced. The operating cash flows occur each year of the project's life. The terminal cash flow (final year) adds the after-tax salvage value of the asset and the recovery of net working capital. Laying a project out in these three stages is the discipline that prevents double-counting or omitting a flow.

Operating cash flow and the depreciation tax shield

Annual operating cash flow (OCF) is computed after tax, and depreciation — though a non-cash expense — matters because it reduces taxes. A convenient formula is OCF = (Revenue − Cash Costs) × (1 − T) + Depreciation × T, where the last term is the depreciation tax shield. Worked example: Northstar's project generates $80,000 of pre-tax operating savings, takes $40,000 of straight-line depreciation, at a 21% tax rate: OCF = $80,000 × 0.79 + $40,000 × 0.21 = $63,200 + $8,400 = $71,600 per year. The shield is real cash — accelerated depreciation, by front-loading it, raises early-year cash flows and NPV.

Net working capital in projects

A project that grows the business usually needs more net working capital (NWC) — additional inventory and receivables, net of payables — to operate. That increase is a cash outflow at the start (and at any point the project scales up), because cash is tied up in the operating cycle. Crucially, NWC is recovered at the end of the project, when inventories are sold and receivables collected, producing a cash inflow in the terminal year. Forgetting either the initial investment or the terminal recovery of NWC is among the most common project-analysis errors.

After-tax salvage value

When an asset is sold at the end of a project, the cash received is the after-tax salvage value, not the gross price, because a gain or loss on sale has tax consequences. The formula: after-tax salvage = sale price − T × (sale price − book value). If the asset is sold for more than book value, the excess is taxed (reducing the inflow); if sold for less, the loss generates a tax saving (increasing the inflow). Worked example: Northstar sells the fully depreciated asset (book value $0) for $20,000: after-tax salvage = $20,000 − 0.21 × ($20,000 − $0) = $15,800.

Replacement decisions and incremental analysis

A replacement decision — keep the old machine or buy a new one — is analyzed on a strictly incremental basis: the relevant flows are the differences between the two alternatives. The new machine's cost is reduced by the after-tax salvage of the old machine sold now; the operating cash flows are the change in OCF (new minus old), including the change in the depreciation tax shield. Framing replacement as "new minus old" keeps the analysis honest and is exactly how a CFO evaluates whether to retire equipment early.

Assembling the project NPV

With the stages in hand, the project's NPV is the present value of the operating cash flows plus the terminal cash flow, minus the initial outlay, discounted at the project's required return (the WACC from Unit 2, risk-adjusted if the project differs from the firm's normal risk). Building the cash-flow timeline first — initial outlay at t=0, OCF in years 1 to n, terminal flows in year n — and only then discounting is the reliable method. The arithmetic of NPV is easy; the judgment about which cash flows belong is where the analysis is won or lost.

Depreciation methods and the timing of the shield

Because the depreciation tax shield is real cash, when depreciation is taken matters. Straight-line spreads it evenly; accelerated methods (and the U.S. MACRS system, or bonus depreciation) front-load it, pulling tax savings into early years where they are worth more in present value. Two projects with identical total depreciation but different timing have different NPVs — the accelerated one is worth more. This is why the choice of depreciation method, though it does not change total taxes over the asset's life, is a genuine value lever in project analysis.

Inflation and consistency in the analysis

A subtle but tested point: the analysis must be internally consistent about inflation. If cash flows are projected in nominal terms (including expected price increases), they must be discounted at a nominal rate; if in real terms, at a real rate. Mixing them — discounting nominal cash flows at a real rate — systematically overstates NPV. Most practical analysis uses nominal cash flows and a nominal WACC. Stating the inflation assumption and applying it consistently to both the cash flows and the discount rate keeps the project valuation honest.

CFO bridge

When a contractor weighs buying a $400,000 crane versus renting, this is the exact analysis: the incremental after-tax operating savings, the depreciation tax shield, the NWC, and the after-tax salvage. The pro-forma and capital-budgeting case workflows in the Apply layer use these same project cash flows — this is where the finance class meets the CFO's equipment decisions.

Practice and recap

  1. Include only incremental, after-tax cash flows: ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs and erosion/synergies; include overhead only if it changes.
  2. Lay out three stages: initial outlay (cost + install + initial NWC − old asset's after-tax salvage), annual OCF, terminal (after-tax salvage + NWC recovery).
  3. OCF = (Revenue − Cash Costs)(1 − T) + Depreciation × T; the depreciation tax shield is real cash.
  4. After-tax salvage = price − T(price − book value); analyze replacements as new minus old.

Recap: project analysis discounts only incremental, after-tax cash flows — sunk costs out, opportunity costs and side effects in; the cash flows fall into the initial outlay (including initial NWC), the annual operating cash flows (OCF = (Rev − Costs)(1 − T) + Dep × T, capturing the depreciation tax shield, e.g. $71,600), and the terminal flow (after-tax salvage, e.g. $15,800, plus NWC recovery); and replacement decisions are evaluated as the difference between the new and old alternatives.

flashcards.back: Incremental + after-tax: a future cash flow that occurs ONLY because of the project. Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs, erosion/synergies; overhead only if it changes.
Initial outlay (cost + install + initial NWC − old asset's after-tax salvage) → annual operating cash flows → terminal (after-tax salvage + NWC recovery).
OCF = (Revenue − Cash Costs) × (1 − T) + Depreciation × T. The last term is the depreciation tax shield (non-cash expense that reduces taxes).
Increase in NWC is an outflow at the start (cash tied up); it is recovered as an inflow in the terminal year. Don't forget either.
Sale price − T × (sale price − book value). Sell above book → taxed; sell below book → tax saving. E.g. $20,000 sale, $0 book, 21%: $15,800.
Sunk cost (already spent) = ignore. Opportunity cost (best alternative use of a resource) = include.
Strictly incremental — analyze new MINUS old: new cost less old asset's after-tax salvage, and the CHANGE in OCF including the change in the depreciation tax shield.

weeks.title: Finance U3·W2 — Pro Formas & Financial Forecasting (NEW)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — building the forward financials

Every other Finance chapter values what exists; forecasting builds what will exist. A pro forma is a projected set of financial statements, and the central CFO question it answers is: if we grow, how much outside financing do we need? This chapter — new to the track — covers percent-of-sales forecasting, the projected income statement and balance sheet, additional funds needed (AFN), the sustainable growth rate, and the lender-ready narrative. It is the chapter that connects corporate finance directly to junior-CFO work, where a forecast becomes the basis of a financing request.

The percent-of-sales method

The workhorse forecasting technique is the percent-of-sales method: most income-statement and balance-sheet items move proportionally with sales, so each is projected as a percentage of forecast sales. On the income statement, costs that vary with volume scale directly. On the balance sheet, operating assets (inventory, receivables, and usually net fixed assets at full capacity) scale with sales, as do spontaneous liabilities — accounts payable and accruals that arise automatically from operations. Items that do not scale automatically include long-term debt, notes payable, and common stock; these change only by explicit financing decisions, which is exactly where the financing gap appears.

The projected income statement

The pro forma income statement starts from forecast sales (the key driver, from management's growth assumption), applies the cost and expense ratios, and works down to projected net income. Net income then splits between dividends (paid out, per the payout ratio d) and retained earnings (kept, per the retention ratio b = 1 − d). The addition to retained earnings — projected net income × retention ratio — is the internal financing the firm generates, and it flows into the projected balance sheet as a credit to equity. The forecast income statement is therefore not just a profit projection; it is the source of internally generated funds.

The projected balance sheet and the plug

The pro forma balance sheet projects assets and spontaneous liabilities by percent-of-sales, adds the new retained earnings to equity, and then confronts the accounting identity: assets must equal liabilities plus equity. Almost always the projected assets exceed the projected liabilities and equity — the firm needs more financing than operations and retained earnings provide. The shortfall is filled by a plug figure: the external financing (new debt or equity) the firm must raise. If instead the firm projects a surplus, the plug parks the excess in cash or pays down debt. The plug is the forecast's punchline — it quantifies the financing decision.

Additional funds needed (AFN)

The shortfall can be computed directly with the AFN equation: AFN = (A*/S0) × ΔS − (L*/S0) × ΔS − M × S1 × (1 − d), where A*/S0 is capital intensity (assets that scale ÷ sales), L*/S0 is spontaneous liabilities ÷ sales, M is the profit margin, S1 is forecast sales, and (1 − d) is retention. The three terms are: the new assets required, less the spontaneous financing from payables/accruals, less the retained earnings generated. Worked example: sales rise from $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 (ΔS = $200,000); capital intensity 0.80; spontaneous liabilities 0.15 of sales; margin 8%; payout 40%. AFN = 0.80 × $200,000 − 0.15 × $200,000 − 0.08 × $1,200,000 × 0.60 = $160,000 − $30,000 − $57,600 = $72,400 of external financing needed.

The sustainable growth rate

How fast can a firm grow without issuing new equity? The sustainable growth rate answers it: g* = (ROE × b) / (1 − ROE × b), where b is the retention ratio. It is the growth that retained earnings and proportional debt can finance while holding the capital structure constant. The related internal growth rate — (ROA × b)/(1 − ROA × b) — is the growth financeable with no external financing at all. Worked example: with ROE of 15% and retention of 60%, g* = (0.15 × 0.60) / (1 − 0.15 × 0.60) = 0.09 / 0.91 ≈ 9.9%. Planned growth above the sustainable rate is precisely why AFN turns positive — the firm is outgrowing its internal financing.

Capital intensity, drivers, and full versus excess capacity

Two refinements sharpen the forecast. Capital intensity (assets ÷ sales) drives how much new investment growth requires — a capital-heavy contractor needs more financing per dollar of growth than an asset-light service firm. And the percent-of-sales assumption that fixed assets scale with sales holds only at full capacity; if the firm has excess capacity, sales can grow with little or no new fixed-asset investment until capacity is reached, sharply lowering AFN. Stating the capacity assumption explicitly is essential, because it can swing the financing need by hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Sensitivity and the lender-ready forecast

A forecast is only as good as its assumptions, so a credible pro forma includes sensitivity analysis — how AFN and net income change if sales growth or the profit margin is higher or lower than the base case (best/base/worst scenarios). The final deliverable for a CFO is a lender-ready narrative: the growth assumption, the resulting financing need, how it will be raised (debt vs equity and the effect on leverage and covenants), and the stress cases. This is exactly the artifact the Apply layer's pro-forma case workflow asks the learner to produce — turning the forecast into a financing conversation.

The financing feedback loop

One subtlety completes the pro forma: raising external financing itself changes the statements. New debt adds interest expense, which lowers net income and thus retained earnings — which slightly raises the financing need again. This financing feedback is why a full pro forma is often solved iteratively (or with simultaneous equations): plug in the financing, recompute interest and retained earnings, and re-solve until the numbers settle. For exam purposes the first-pass AFN is usually sufficient, but recognizing the feedback loop explains why a real forecast is built in a spreadsheet rather than a single calculation.

CFO bridge

The Meridian Building Group pro-forma workflow in the Apply layer runs this exact analysis on a fictional contractor: project the statements, compute AFN, explain the funding gap to a lender, and stress-test growth and margin. This chapter is the most direct bridge from the finance class to the junior-CFO seat — a pro forma is how a controller-turned-CFO asks the bank for money with a straight face.

Practice and recap

  1. Forecast with percent-of-sales: scale operating assets and spontaneous liabilities (AP/accruals) with sales; debt, notes payable, and stock do NOT scale automatically.
  2. Build the projected income statement to net income, split by payout/retention; the addition to retained earnings is internal financing.
  3. Project the balance sheet; the plug = external financing needed (or surplus). Compute AFN = (A*/S₀)ΔS − (L*/S₀)ΔS − M·S₁·(1 − d).
  4. Find the sustainable growth rate g* = (ROE·b)/(1 − ROE·b); adjust for full vs excess capacity; run sensitivity and write the lender-ready narrative.

Recap: a pro forma projects the statements by percent-of-sales — operating assets and spontaneous liabilities scale with sales while debt and equity do not, exposing a financing gap; that gap is the plug, computed directly as AFN = (A*/S₀)ΔS − (L*/S₀)ΔS − M·S₁·(1 − d) (e.g. $72,400); the sustainable growth rate g* = (ROE·b)/(1 − ROE·b) (e.g. 9.9%) is the growth internal funds and proportional debt can finance, so growth above it drives AFN positive; and capacity assumptions, sensitivity analysis, and a lender-ready narrative complete a forecast a CFO can take to the bank.
