weeks.title: Finance U3·W3 — Working Capital & the Cash Conversion Cycle
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the cash caught in operations

A profitable firm can still run out of cash. The reason is working capital — the cash tied up in inventory and receivables before customers pay, net of what suppliers finance. Managing it well frees cash and lowers the financing a growing business needs (the AFN from last week). This chapter covers net working capital, the cash conversion cycle, and the management of cash, receivables, inventory, and payables — the day-to-day finance that separates a solvent contractor from one that bounces payroll despite a full backlog.

Working capital defined

Working capital is the firm's short-term resources and obligations. Net working capital (NWC) = current assets − current liabilities; it measures the liquidity cushion funding day-to-day operations. Working-capital policy balances two risks: too little (illiquidity — the inability to pay obligations as they come due) and too much (idle assets earning no return). The art is holding just enough inventory, receivables, and cash to operate smoothly while financing them as cheaply as the risk allows.

The operating cycle and cash conversion cycle

Two cycles describe how cash moves through operations. The operating cycle is the time from acquiring inventory to collecting cash from its sale: days inventory outstanding (DIO) + days sales outstanding (DSO). The cash conversion cycle (CCC) subtracts the financing suppliers provide: CCC = DIO + DSO − days payable outstanding (DPO). The CCC is the number of days the firm's own cash is tied up. Worked example: DIO 60 days + DSO 45 days − DPO 30 days = 75 days of cash locked in the cycle. Shortening any component frees cash.

Computing the components

Each component is a turnover-based ratio. DIO = inventory ÷ (COGS ÷ 365) — how long inventory sits. DSO = accounts receivable ÷ (sales ÷ 365) — how long customers take to pay. DPO = accounts payable ÷ (COGS ÷ 365) — how long the firm takes to pay suppliers. A firm reduces its CCC by turning inventory faster, collecting receivables sooner, or (carefully) paying suppliers later. For a contractor, retainage and slow owner payments stretch DSO dramatically, which is why construction is so working-capital-intensive — the CCC concept directly explains the cash strain.

Cash management

Firms hold cash for the transaction, precautionary, and (less so) speculative motives, but idle cash earns little, so the goal is a target balance that meets needs without excess. Managers accelerate collections (lockboxes, electronic payment) and manage disbursement timing, exploiting — within ethical limits — the float between when a payment is recorded and when cash actually moves. A cash budget (the 13-week forecast a CFO lives by) projects inflows and outflows to reveal shortfalls before they happen — the link between working-capital management and the cash forecasting in the CFO lane.

Receivables and inventory

Receivables management sets the credit policy — to whom credit is granted, the terms (e.g., 2/10 net 30), and the collection effort — trading higher sales against the cost of carrying and potentially losing receivables. A cash discount like 2/10 net 30 carries a steep implicit annual cost if not taken, so customers usually should pay early and firms should evaluate offering it. Inventory management balances ordering costs against carrying costs — the economic order quantity (EOQ) minimizes their total — while just-in-time systems cut inventory (and DIO) by coordinating closely with suppliers. Both aim to support sales with the least cash tied up.

Payables and short-term financing

On the financing side, payables management uses supplier credit as a source of (often free) short-term financing — but stretching payables too far risks supplier relationships and forfeits cash discounts. When operations need more short-term cash than payables provide, firms draw on a line of credit, issue commercial paper (large, creditworthy firms), or factor/pledge receivables. Each source has a cost and a risk profile, and the CFO chooses the mix that funds the cash conversion cycle at the lowest sustainable cost — the practical counterpart to the capital-structure decisions from earlier units.

Working-capital financing strategies

Finally, the firm chooses how to finance current assets. A conservative strategy funds even temporary needs with long-term capital — lower risk (no refinancing pressure) but higher cost. An aggressive strategy funds some permanent current assets with short-term debt — lower cost but higher refinancing and interest-rate risk. The matching (maturity-hedging) principle finances temporary needs with short-term sources and permanent needs with long-term sources — aligning the life of the financing with the life of the asset. The choice trades cost against the risk of a cash squeeze, the recurring theme of short-term finance.

Float and the mechanics of collection

Cash management exploits float — the gap between when a payment is initiated and when the cash actually clears. Collection float delays the firm's receipt of customer payments; speeding it up (via lockboxes that receive payments directly at a bank, and electronic transfer) accelerates available cash. Disbursement float works the other way. As electronic payments shrink float, the emphasis shifts from playing the float to forecasting accuracy and concentrating cash efficiently. The principle endures: getting cash in faster and timing payments out sensibly improves liquidity without changing profitability. Concentration banking then pools cash from multiple accounts into one, so the firm can invest or deploy its full balance rather than leaving idle pockets scattered across banks.

Liquidity reserves and short-term investments

Firms hold a liquidity reserve against uncertainty, parking temporarily idle cash in marketable securities — Treasury bills, money-market instruments — that earn a return while staying highly liquid and low-risk. Sizing the reserve trades the cost of holding low-yield liquid assets against the risk of a cash shortfall. A contractor with lumpy, milestone-based cash flows needs a larger buffer than a steady-revenue business, which ties working-capital policy back to the firm's specific cash-flow pattern — the same logic the CFO lane's cash-forecasting applies.

CFO bridge

The cash conversion cycle is the single most useful concept a junior CFO can carry into a contractor's office: it explains why a company can be profitable on paper yet cash-starved, and it points straight at the levers — collect retainage, turn jobs faster, manage subs' payment terms. The CFO lane's cash-forecasting and lender-conversation workflows build directly on this chapter.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute net working capital (current assets − current liabilities) and balance illiquidity risk against idle-asset cost.
  2. Calculate the cash conversion cycle: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO (e.g., 60 + 45 − 30 = 75 days); compute each from turnover.
  3. Manage cash (target balance, float, cash budget), receivables (credit terms, 2/10 net 30), inventory (EOQ, JIT), and payables (discounts vs stretching).
  4. Choose a financing strategy: conservative (safe, costly) vs aggressive (cheap, risky) vs matching (maturity-hedge).

Recap: working capital is the cash tied up in operations, and the cash conversion cycle (DIO + DSO − DPO, e.g. 75 days) measures how long the firm's own cash is locked up; shortening it — faster inventory turns, quicker collections, sensible payment timing — frees cash and lowers AFN; cash, receivables (2/10 net 30 credit terms), inventory (EOQ/JIT), and payables are each managed to minimize tied-up cash; and the firm finances current assets along a conservative–aggressive spectrum, with the matching principle aligning financing maturity to asset life.

weeks.title: Finance U3·W4 — Financial Planning, Ratios, DuPont & CFO Decision-Making
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — reading a company the way a CFO does

The course closes where the CFO's work begins: integrating everything — statements, ratios, forecasts, capital budgeting, and financing — into judgment about a company's health and direction. This capstone covers the full ratio toolkit, the DuPont decomposition that explains why returns are what they are, the financial-planning process that ties the pieces together, and the limitations a careful analyst keeps in mind. It is the chapter that turns a finance student into someone who can sit across from a lender or an owner and explain the numbers.

The five categories of ratios

Financial ratios fall into five families. Liquidity ratios — the current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) and the stricter quick ratio (excluding inventory) — measure the ability to meet short-term obligations. Activity/efficiency ratios (inventory, receivables, and total-asset turnover) measure how productively assets are used. Leverage/solvency ratios (debt-to-equity, debt ratio, times-interest-earned) measure financial risk and the ability to service debt. Profitability ratios (net profit margin, ROA, ROE) measure returns. Market ratios (price-earnings, market-to-book) relate price to fundamentals. A single ratio is noise; the categories together tell the story.

DuPont analysis — decomposing ROE

Return on equity is the headline number, and DuPont analysis explains it by decomposition. The three-step DuPont: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier — that is, profitability × efficiency × leverage. Worked example: a net margin of 8%, asset turnover of 1.5, and an equity multiplier of 2.0 give ROE = 0.08 × 1.5 × 2.0 = 24%. The power of DuPont is diagnostic: two firms with the same ROE may earn it very differently — one through high margins, another through heavy leverage — and the decomposition reveals where the return comes from and which lever to pull.

Extended DuPont and the leverage warning

The five-step (extended) DuPont breaks margin and the equity multiplier further to separate operating performance from the effects of interest and taxes, isolating how financing and the tax burden shape ROE. A central insight emerges: ROE can be raised by increasing the equity multiplier — i.e., by taking on more debt — but that lifts return by adding financial risk, not by improving the business. A rising ROE driven purely by leverage is a warning, not a triumph. DuPont keeps the analyst honest about the source of a return.

Common-size, trend, and benchmark analysis

Ratios gain meaning through comparison. Common-size statements express every income-statement line as a percentage of sales and every balance-sheet line as a percentage of total assets, making firms of different sizes comparable and revealing structural shifts. Trend (horizontal) analysis tracks ratios over several years to spot direction. Benchmarking compares the firm to industry peers and to its own history. A current ratio of 1.4 is neither good nor bad until set against the prior year and the industry norm — comparison is what converts a number into a judgment.

The financial-planning process

Financial planning ties the course together into a process. It begins with the strategic plan (the firm's direction), translates into an operating plan and budgets, projects a cash budget (short-term liquidity) and pro forma statements (the forecast and AFN from Week 2), and tests the plan with sensitivity and scenario analysis. The plan is iterative: if the pro forma reveals an unaffordable financing need or a covenant breach, management revises growth, payout, or the capital structure and re-runs it. Planning is how a CFO turns strategy into financeable, monitored numbers.

The CFO's integrative judgment

The CFO's distinctive skill is integration: reading the ratios to diagnose health, using the forecast to anticipate financing needs, applying capital budgeting to allocate investment, and choosing the capital structure to fund it — then explaining the whole to lenders, owners, and the board. A weak current ratio plus a positive AFN plus a tight times-interest-earned, taken together, tell a coherent story about liquidity risk that no single metric conveys. This synthesis — turning analysis into a decision and a conversation — is the competency the entire Finance track, and the CFO lane, is built to develop.

The limitations of ratio analysis

A careful analyst respects the limits. Ratios rest on accounting data that can be shaped by policy choices (depreciation methods, inventory costing) and by window dressing near period-end. Historical figures may not predict the future; seasonal businesses distort point-in-time balances; and industry benchmarks can mislead for a diversified firm. Ratios raise questions rather than answer them — a striking ratio is a prompt to investigate, not a verdict. Knowing these limits is what separates mechanical ratio computation from genuine financial analysis.

From ratios to value: free cash flow

The bridge from ratio analysis to valuation (Unit 2) is free cash flow — the cash a firm generates after funding operations and necessary investment, available to all capital providers. FCF = operating cash flow − capital expenditures − increase in net working capital. A firm can show strong accounting profit yet weak free cash flow if it is consuming cash in capex and working capital — exactly the gap the cash conversion cycle and the pro forma reveal. Because value (the DCF of Unit 2) rests on free cash flow, the analyst who can move from the ratios to the cash a business actually throws off is the one who can value it.

Profitability anatomy: ROA, ROE, and margins

Profitability deserves a closer look because the ratios interlock. Net profit margin measures profit per dollar of sales; ROA (net income ÷ assets) measures profit per dollar of assets, combining margin and asset turnover; and ROE (net income ÷ equity) measures profit per dollar of owners' capital, adding leverage to ROA. The chain ROE = ROA × equity multiplier shows precisely how leverage converts an asset return into an equity return. Knowing which denominator each ratio uses — sales, assets, or equity — is what prevents the common error of comparing returns that do not measure the same thing.

CFO bridge

This capstone is the analytical spine of the junior-CFO role: the board-reporting, lender-conversation, and covenant-monitoring workflows in the CFO lane all draw on DuPont, the ratio categories, and the planning process. The Finance track ends exactly where the controller-to-CFO transition begins — explaining a company's numbers and deciding what to do about them.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the five ratio categories: liquidity, activity, leverage/solvency, profitability, market.
  2. Decompose ROE with DuPont: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier (e.g. 8% × 1.5 × 2.0 = 24%); watch for ROE lifted only by leverage.
  3. Compare via common-size, trend, and benchmark analysis; run the planning process (strategic → operating → cash budget → pro forma → sensitivity).
  4. Integrate ratios + forecast + capital budgeting + structure into a CFO decision; respect the limitations of ratio analysis.

Recap: the five ratio categories (liquidity, activity, leverage, profitability, market) together diagnose a company; DuPont decomposes ROE into margin × turnover × leverage (8% × 1.5 × 2.0 = 24%), revealing the source of returns and warning when leverage alone is doing the work; common-size, trend, and benchmark comparisons convert numbers into judgment; the financial-planning process links strategy to the cash budget and pro forma; and the CFO's integrative judgment — bounded by the real limits of ratio analysis — turns all of it into decisions and conversations with lenders and owners.

weeks.title: Finance U4·W1 — Job Cost Architecture: Cost Codes, Burden, Committed Cost & the Sub-Ledger Tie
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the applied track starts here

Units 1 through 3 built the corporate-finance spine: time value, valuation, cost of capital, capital budgeting, forecasting. Units 4 through 7 take that spine and drive it through a contractor’s general ledger. Everything here is CMA Part 1 content wearing work clothes. Job costing is Part 1-D Cost Management. WIP and revenue are Part 1-A External Financial Reporting. Close and cutoff controls are Part 1-E Internal Controls. Budgets, draw schedules and overhead absorption are Part 1-B Planning, Budgeting and Forecasting. A rep on a construction workpaper is not a detour from the exam — it is the same skill, tagged the same way, and it moves the same readiness number.

All examples use fictional companies: Meridian Building Group LLC (homebuilding and general contracting), Riverton Partners LLC (land development), and Northstar Services LLC (labor and equipment). Every dollar figure in this unit is invented.

The job is the cost object

In manufacturing, the cost object is a batch or a process. In construction it is the job — a contract, a lot, a building, or a phase — and the accounting system is a textbook job-order costing system. Every dollar of cost must answer three questions before it posts: which job, which cost code, and which cost type. Miss any one and the cost lands somewhere that cannot be analyzed.

  • Job number — the contract or lot. This is the profit-center dimension.
  • Cost code — the scope of work, usually a division-and-item code (03-300 concrete, 06-100 rough framing, 15-400 plumbing). This is the budget-comparison dimension.
  • Cost type — L labor, M material, S subcontract, E equipment, O other. This is the behavior dimension, and it is what lets you tell an overrun caused by hours from one caused by price.

The three together form the cost-code key. A budget is loaded at this key, actuals post at this key, and every variance report is a join on this key. If field staff can post to a job without a cost code, the system will happily accumulate an unanalyzable pile.

Direct, indirect and the burden calculation

Direct costs trace to one job: the framing crew’s hours, the lumber package, the plumbing subcontract. Indirect construction costs benefit many jobs — superintendents, trucks, small tools, jobsite trailers, project managers — and are absorbed to jobs through a rate (Unit 7 Week 4 builds that rate and its variances). General and administrative costs — the office, the controller, the owner’s salary — are period costs and never touch a job.

Self-performed labor is the trap inside the trap, because the wage is only part of the cost. Burden must be applied at the moment payroll posts to the job, not annually in an adjusting entry. Meridian’s burden build:

On Job 2418 (Willow Bend custom residence) the framing crew earned $60,000 of gross wages. Burden = $60,000 × 30.00% = $18,000, so the job carries $78,000 of burdened framing labor, not $60,000. A contractor who bids using unburdened labor bids 23.1% light on every self-perform line ($18,000 ÷ $78,000), and the gap shows up later as gross-profit fade with no identifiable cause.

The job cost ledger versus the general ledger

The job cost system is a sub-ledger. The general ledger holds one or a few control accounts — work in process, cost of revenue — and the sub-ledger holds the detail by job and cost code. The unbreakable rule is the same one that governs accounts payable and fixed assets: the sub-ledger must foot to the control account, every period, to the penny.

Total job cost ledger$235,950

The GL work-in-process account for Job 2418 reads $238,700. The difference is $2,750, and there is exactly one acceptable response: find it. Here the cause was a plumbing invoice posted directly to the WIP account with a job number but no cost code, so it hit the GL and never reached the sub-ledger. The fix is not a plug entry; it is re-coding the invoice and then turning off the ability to post to WIP without a cost code. A reconciling item you cannot name is an error you have not found yet.

The trap: an “ending balance” column that is not cumulative

Job cost reports are exported constantly, and the column headings lie more often than you would believe. Meridian’s September export carries a column labeled Ending Balance. It is not an inception-to-date balance. It is period activity — costs posted in September only. For Job 2418 that column totals $54,050 (plumbing $29,750 plus electrical $24,300), while the true inception-to-date figure is $235,950.

Now watch what that does downstream. Against a total budget of $295,000:

  • Correct percent complete = $235,950 ÷ $295,000 = 79.98%.
  • Percent complete using the mislabeled column = $54,050 ÷ $295,000 = 18.32%.

A job that is four-fifths built reports as barely started, earned revenue collapses, and the WIP schedule swings by more than sixty points of completion on a single job. The defense is procedural, not clever: before any export becomes an input to a schedule, foot it and tie it. Sum the column and compare it to the GL control account. $54,050 does not equal $238,700, so the column is not what its heading claims, and you find that out in ten seconds instead of at the audit.

Committed cost — the number that is not in the ledger

The job cost ledger is history. The forecast needs committed cost: signed subcontracts and issued purchase orders that are not yet invoiced. Job 2418 carries $41,300 of open commitments, so:

  • Projected cost at completion = $235,950 incurred + $41,300 committed = $277,250.
  • Versus budget $295,000, that is $17,750 favorable — if nothing else is missing.

The discipline is asking what is missing. Committed cost only covers scope that has been bought out. Unbought scope carries no commitment and therefore no visibility, which is why the cost-at-completion estimate must always be built as incurred + committed + estimate of unbought scope. Unit 4 Week 4 builds that estimate to complete properly.

Data flow: where cost enters the system

Costs reach a job through five doors, and each door needs a control: payroll (time coded by job and cost code, then burdened), accounts payable (invoice matched to a subcontract or purchase order, coded on entry), subcontract pay applications (schedule-of-values based, with retention withheld), equipment and internal charges (an hourly or daily rate charged to the job and credited to the equipment pool), and journal entries (reclasses and accruals). Any door that can bypass coding is a hole in the job cost system. The most common hole is the credit-card feed that posts to an expense account with no job dimension at all.

A second architectural point matters for reporting: the job cost system and the general ledger are often different applications, with different charts of accounts and different period-close mechanics. That is normal and workable, but it makes the crosswalk a formal deliverable — a mapping from every job cost account to a GL account, maintained under change control, tested at every close. When someone adds a cost code and forgets the crosswalk, the cost posts to the job and disappears from the GL, or vice versa, and the difference shows up as an unexplained sub-ledger break next month.

Reading a job cost report like a controller

A job cost report has four columns that matter and one habit that separates a controller from a bookkeeper. The columns are original budget, approved revisions, cost to date, and cost at completion. The habit is reading them by cost code, not in total, because totals hide offsetting errors. On Job 2418 the concrete code came in $4,200 under and the plumbing code $6,900 over; in total the job looks $2,700 over, which is a number nobody can act on. Broken out, one is a buyout win to bank and the other is a scope question to answer before the same subcontractor bids the next four houses.

Three questions get asked on every line that moves. Is it price or quantity? A material line that grew because lumber prices rose is a market event; one that grew because the takeoff was short is an estimating defect that will repeat on every similar house. Is it in scope or out? Out-of-scope work performed without an executed change order is cost with no matching revenue, and it converts directly into gross-profit fade (Unit 4 Week 4). Is the budget still right? A budget that has never been revised on a job that has been running six months is not a control — it is a decoration.

Finally, the report has to be read against the schedule. Cost to date of 79.98% on a house the superintendent says is at drywall is coherent. Cost to date of 79.98% on a house still at foundation means either the costs are miscoded to the wrong job or the budget is badly wrong, and both are findable in an afternoon. The cheapest reconciliation in construction accounting is walking the job with the report in your hand.

CMA bridge

Everything above is Part 1-D Cost Management: job-order costing, direct versus indirect classification, cost-object definition, and the sub-ledger-to-control-account relationship. The burden rate is a predetermined overhead rate applied to a cost driver. The sub-ledger tie is the same reconciliation logic Part 1-E tests as a control activity. Do the job cost rep on a Tuesday and you have done the exam rep.

Practice and recap

  1. Code every cost to job + cost code + cost type. A cost with only a job number is an unanalyzable cost.
  2. Burden self-perform labor at the moment payroll posts: $60,000 wages × 30.00% = $18,000 burden = $78,000 burdened.
  3. Foot the job cost sub-ledger to the GL control account every close. $235,950 versus $238,700 is a $2,750 error to be named, not plugged.
  4. Never trust a column heading. An “Ending Balance” column that is period activity turned 79.98% complete into 18.32% complete.
  5. Forecast with incurred + committed + unbought: $235,950 + $41,300 = $277,250 against a $295,000 budget.

Recap: construction accounting is job-order costing with a sub-ledger, and the controller’s job is to keep the coding key intact, the burden applied, the sub-ledger tied to the control account to the penny, and every exported column footed before it feeds a schedule — because a mislabeled export column is a bigger threat to reported gross profit than any estimating error.

flashcards.back: Job number + cost code + cost type (L/M/S/E/O). Budgets load at this key, actuals post at this key, and every variance report joins on it. A cost with only a job number cannot be analyzed.
Direct = traces to one job. Indirect construction = supers, trucks, small tools, PMs — absorbed to jobs via a rate. G&A = office/period cost, never touches a job.
FICA 7.65% + FUTA/SUTA 1.85% + workers' comp 11.50% + GL insurance 2.00% + benefits 5.00% + PTO 2.00% = 30.00% of gross wages.
$60,000 gross framing wages × 30.00% = $18,000 burden → $78,000 burdened labor on the job. Bidding unburdened understates the labor line by $18,000 ÷ $78,000 = 23.1%.
The job cost sub-ledger must foot to the GL control account (WIP / cost of revenue) to the penny every period. Job 2418: ledger $235,950 vs GL $238,700 = $2,750 to be NAMED, not plugged.

An export column labeled Ending Balance may be PERIOD activity. Job 2418: $54,050 (period) vs $235,950 (ITD). % complete on a $295,000 budget: 18.32% (wrong) vs 79.98% (right). Foot the export and tie it to the GL first.
Signed subcontracts and issued POs not yet invoiced. Job 2418: $235,950 incurred + $41,300 committed = $277,250 projected vs $295,000 budget = $17,750 favorable — only if all scope is bought out.
Incurred + committed + estimate of UNBOUGHT scope. Committed cost only covers bought-out work, so a projection using incurred + committed alone silently omits everything not yet awarded.

questions.explain: $60,000 × 30.00% = $18,000 burden; $60,000 + $18,000 = $78,000. Burden is applied when payroll posts, not in a year-end entry.

choices: Post a $2,750 plug to the sub-ledger
questions.explain: A reconciling item you cannot name is an unfound error. Here it was an invoice posted to WIP with a job number but no cost code — fix the coding and close the control gap.

questions.explain: $54,050 ÷ $295,000 = 18.32%; $235,950 ÷ $295,000 = 79.98%. Foot every export and tie it to the GL before it feeds a schedule.

questions.explain: $235,950 + $41,300 = $277,250; $295,000 − $277,250 = $17,750 favorable, valid only if all remaining scope is bought out.

choices: A jobsite superintendent covering four active jobs

It determines the customer's retainage percentage
It sets the general ledger account for cash
It is required to file the contract

choices: Job cost is understated and the sub-ledger no longer explains the control account

weeks.title: Finance U4·W2 — WIP and Cost-to-Cost Percent Complete
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the schedule that runs the company

The work-in-process schedule is the single most important workpaper a contractor produces. It is where cost accounting becomes revenue recognition. It drives the income statement, two balance-sheet lines, the surety’s bonding decision and the bank’s covenant test. A contractor with a wrong WIP schedule does not have small errors — it has a wrong income statement, because in construction revenue is derived, not recorded. Nobody sends an invoice that equals revenue. Revenue is computed from cost.

The cost-to-cost measure

Under the input method known as cost-to-cost, progress toward satisfying a performance obligation is measured by the ratio of costs incurred to total costs expected:

Percent complete = cost incurred to date ÷ estimated cost at completion (EAC)

Then, in strict order:

  1. Earned revenue = percent complete × total contract price (inception-to-date).
  2. Cost of revenue = cost incurred to date (inception-to-date — you do not compute it, you take it).
  3. Earned gross profit = earned revenue − cost incurred to date, which also equals percent complete × total estimated gross profit.
  4. Current-period amounts = inception-to-date amounts − prior inception-to-date amounts.

Everything is inception-to-date first and periodized second. Trying to compute a month’s revenue directly is the most common way to lose the audit trail, because the moment an estimate changes the prior periods have to be absorbed through a catch-up (Unit 4 Week 4).

The three inputs, and which one is an estimate

Only three numbers feed the calculation: contract price, cost incurred to date, and estimated cost at completion. The first two are facts you can audit — the executed contract plus approved change orders, and the job cost sub-ledger tied to the GL (Week 1). The third is an estimate, and it is the only judgment in the whole schedule. That is why the auditor spends most of the fieldwork on it and why every controller-level control in construction ultimately points at the EAC.

Contract price must include approved change orders only. Unapproved change orders and claims enter the transaction price only under the variable-consideration constraint (Unit 5 Week 1). Cost incurred must include everything: burdened self-perform labor, subcontract costs gross of retention withheld, materials delivered and installed, allocated indirect construction overhead, and equipment charges.

Worked example — Harbor Row Townhomes Phase 2

Meridian Building Group, contract HR-2:

  • Contract price including approved change orders: $4,250,000
  • Estimated cost at completion: $3,612,500 → estimated gross profit $637,500, a 15.00% margin
  • Cost incurred to date: $2,348,125
  • Billings to date (gross of retention): $2,900,000

Percent complete = $2,348,125 ÷ $3,612,500 = 65.00%.
Earned revenue = 65.00% × $4,250,000 = $2,762,500.
Earned gross profit = $2,762,500 − $2,348,125 = $414,375, which checks against 65.00% × $637,500 = $414,375.
Billings $2,900,000 exceed earned revenue $2,762,500, so the job is overbilled by $137,500 — a contract liability, covered in Week 3.

The trap: taking percent complete on revenue instead of cost

This is the error that quietly destroys a WIP schedule, and it looks completely reasonable to whoever makes it. The reasoning goes: we have billed $2,900,000 of a $4,250,000 contract, so we are 68.24% complete. Trace the consequences.

  • Billings-based percent complete = $2,900,000 ÷ $4,250,000 = 68.24%.
  • Earned revenue = 68.24% × $4,250,000 = $2,900,000 — exactly the billings. The calculation is circular. Revenue can never differ from billings, so the over/under billing column is structurally zero on every job, forever.
  • Earned gross profit = 68.24% × $637,500 = $435,000, versus the correct $414,375. Gross profit is overstated by $20,625 on this job alone.

Two things make this lethal. First, it defeats the entire purpose of the schedule: the over/under billing analysis exists to reveal the difference between what you billed and what you earned, and a revenue-based measure defines that difference out of existence. Second, it is self-concealing — the schedule still foots, the balance sheet still balances, and nothing looks wrong. The tell is structural, not arithmetic: if the overbilling and underbilling columns are all zeros, the percent complete is not being taken on cost.

The diagnostic is a single sentence. Percent complete measures inputs consumed, not invoices sent. Billing is a contractual and cash-timing event governed by the schedule of values and the owner’s payment terms; it has nothing to do with how much of the work has been performed. A contractor can bill 90% of a contract in month one if the schedule of values is front-loaded (Unit 7 Week 1), and that changes cash, not revenue.

The multi-job WIP schedule and its footing checks

Three of Meridian’s open contracts at September 30:

Meridian Building Group — contracts in progress, September 30
ContractContract priceEACCost to date% completeEarned revenueEarned GPBilled to dateOverUnder
HR-2 Harbor Row Ph 2$4,250,000$3,612,500$2,348,12565.00%$2,762,500$414,375$2,900,000$137,500—
AC-1 Ashford Commons sitework$1,800,000$1,530,000$1,147,50075.00%$1,350,000$202,500$1,282,000—$68,000
LR-4 Lakeshore Ridge clubhouse$960,000$830,000$415,00050.00%$480,000$65,000$452,500—$27,500
Totals$7,010,000$5,972,500$3,910,625$4,592,500$681,875$4,634,500$137,500$95,500

Four footing checks must pass before this schedule leaves your desk, and they take about ninety seconds:

  1. Gross profit ties across: earned revenue $4,592,500 − cost to date $3,910,625 = $681,875, which equals the earned GP column total.
  2. Over/under ties to the billing gap: billed $4,634,500 − earned $4,592,500 = $42,000, and overbillings $137,500 − underbillings $95,500 = $42,000.
  3. Cost column ties to the GL: the cost-to-date total plus costs on contracts completed during the year must equal cost of revenue on the income statement.
  4. Revenue column ties to the GL: earned revenue on open contracts plus revenue on contracts completed must equal contract revenue on the income statement.

Note that the balance sheet shows $95,500 of contract assets and $137,500 of contract liabilities, gross. They are not netted to $42,000. Netting is a presentation error and it hides an overbilled job funding an underbilled one — exactly the pattern a surety underwriter is looking for.

Percent complete above 100% and other impossibilities

Automated WIP schedules produce absurdities, and the controller’s job is to catch them before the lender does. A percent complete above 100% means cost to date exceeds the EAC — the estimate was never updated and the job has already blown through it; the EAC is stale, not the cost. Earned revenue above the contract price is the same defect one column over. Negative earned gross profit on a job with a positive estimated margin means either the percent complete moved backwards (an EAC increase, which is legitimate and produces a catch-up) or costs were miscoded onto the job. And a job at 100% complete with an open commitment balance means either the commitment should have been closed or the job is not actually finished. None of these are rounding issues; each is a specific, findable posting or estimating problem.

Periodizing: turning inception-to-date into this month

Every figure above is cumulative. The income statement needs a period, and the conversion is mechanical: this period = inception-to-date now − inception-to-date at the prior close. For HR-2, if Q1 closed at $2,762,500 of earned revenue and $2,348,125 of cost, and the prior quarter had closed at $2,145,000 and $1,823,500, then the quarter’s revenue is $617,500 and the quarter’s cost of revenue is $524,625, giving $92,875 of gross profit for the quarter.

Two rules protect this. Freeze the prior column. The prior inception-to-date figures must come from the closed prior-period schedule, not from a re-computation using today’s estimates — recomputing silently absorbs an estimate change into a prior period, which is exactly what the standard forbids. Keep every closed WIP schedule. The archive of quarterly WIP schedules is the audit trail for every catch-up entry, the source data for the fade analysis in Week 4, and the first thing an auditor or surety analyst asks for.

Input methods, output methods, and when cost-to-cost misleads

Cost-to-cost is an input method: it infers progress from resources consumed. Output methods measure progress directly — units delivered, milestones achieved, surveys of work performed, physical quantities in place. Both are acceptable; the requirement is that the measure faithfully depicts transfer of control, and that the choice is applied consistently to similar contracts.

Cost-to-cost breaks down in three recognizable situations. Front-loaded costs: a job whose early scope is expensive relative to its value — heavy sitework, deep foundations, a large mobilization — reads as more complete than it is. Inefficiency: costs incurred because of rework or a labor overrun increase the numerator without advancing the work, so a job that is going badly reports faster progress, which is precisely backwards. Materials on site but not installed: a delivered generator or curtain-wall package adds cost without transferring anything, and Unit 5 Week 1 shows the adjustment the standard requires.

The practical response is not to abandon cost-to-cost — it is auditable and cheap — but to cross-check it. On a residential job, compare percent complete to the construction milestone the superintendent reports. On a unit-price job, compare it to quantities placed. When the two measures disagree by more than a few points, one of them is wrong, and finding out which is a far better use of an afternoon than refining the schedule’s formatting.

CMA bridge

Cost-to-cost is Part 1-A External Financial Reporting — revenue recognized over time using an input method — sitting directly on Part 1-D Cost Management, because the numerator is the job cost accumulation from Week 1. The exam asks you to compute earned revenue and gross profit for a period from contract price, cost incurred and estimated cost to complete; the WIP schedule is that computation for a whole company at once, with footing checks attached.

Practice and recap

  1. Percent complete = cost to date ÷ EAC. Never billings ÷ contract.
  2. Earned revenue = % complete × contract price, inception-to-date; period revenue = ITD minus prior ITD.
  3. Earned GP = earned revenue − cost to date = % complete × estimated total GP. Prove it both ways every time.
  4. Overbillings and underbillings are presented gross: $137,500 liability and $95,500 asset, not $42,000 net.
  5. Run the four footing checks, then scan for percent complete > 100%, revenue > contract price and negative GP on profitable jobs.

Recap: the WIP schedule converts job cost into revenue through the cost-to-cost ratio; contract price and cost to date are facts while the EAC is the only estimate, so the EAC is where all the risk lives; measuring completion on billings instead of cost is circular, forces revenue to equal billings, zeroes the over/under columns and overstated Harbor Row’s gross profit by $20,625; and a schedule is not finished until earned GP, the billing gap, and both GL ties have been footed.

flashcards.back: % complete = cost incurred to date ÷ estimated cost at completion (EAC). It measures INPUTS CONSUMED, never invoices sent.

1) % complete = CTD ÷ EAC. 2) Earned revenue = % × contract price (ITD). 3) Cost of revenue = CTD (taken, not computed). 4) Earned GP = earned revenue − CTD = % × estimated total GP. Period amounts = ITD − prior ITD.

flashcards.front: Trap — % complete on revenue instead of cost
flashcards.back: Billings ÷ contract = $2,900,000 ÷ $4,250,000 = 68.24%. Earned revenue then equals billings EXACTLY — circular — so over/under billing is structurally zero on every job. GP becomes $435,000 vs the correct $414,375: overstated $20,625.

flashcards.front: The tell for a revenue-based % complete
flashcards.back: The overbilling and underbilling columns are all zeros. The schedule still foots and the balance sheet still balances — the defect is structural, not arithmetic.

flashcards.front: The only estimate in the WIP schedule
flashcards.back: The EAC. Contract price (executed contract + APPROVED change orders) and cost to date (sub-ledger tied to GL) are auditable facts. All estimation risk — and all audit attention — sits on the EAC.
Contract assets $95,500 and contract liabilities $137,500 are presented GROSS, not netted to $42,000. Netting hides an overbilled job funding an underbilled one — exactly what a surety looks for.

(1) Earned revenue − cost to date = earned GP column. (2) Billed − earned = overbillings − underbillings ($4,634,500 − $4,592,500 = $42,000 = $137,500 − $95,500). (3) Cost column ties to cost of revenue. (4) Revenue column ties to contract revenue.

questions.q: Harbor Row Ph 2: contract $4,250,000, EAC $3,612,500, cost to date $2,348,125. Earned revenue to date is:
Using the same facts, earned gross profit to date is:
questions.explain: $2,762,500 − $2,348,125 = $414,375, which equals 65.00% × the $637,500 estimated total gross profit.

questions.q: A controller computes percent complete as billings ÷ contract price ($2,900,000 ÷ $4,250,000 = 68.24%). What happens to the over/under billing column?
choices: It becomes structurally zero on every job, because earned revenue is forced to equal billings
questions.explain: 68.24% × $4,250,000 = $2,900,000 = the billings. The calculation is circular, so earned revenue can never differ from billings and the analysis is destroyed.

questions.q: Under that same billings-based error, gross profit on Harbor Row is misstated by:
questions.explain: 68.24% × $637,500 = $435,000 versus the correct $414,375 — a $20,625 overstatement.

questions.q: A WIP schedule shows total billings $4,634,500 and total earned revenue $4,592,500. Overbillings total $137,500. Underbillings must total:
questions.explain: Billed − earned = $42,000 net, and overbillings − underbillings must equal that: $137,500 − $95,500 = $42,000.

questions.q: Those same balances should appear on the balance sheet as:
choices: A $95,500 contract asset and a $137,500 contract liability, presented gross
questions.explain: Contract assets and liabilities are presented gross. Netting conceals an overbilled job financing an underbilled one.

questions.q: A WIP schedule shows a job at 108% complete. The most likely cause is:
choices: The EAC is stale and has not been raised as costs grew
The contract price was recorded twice
questions.explain: Percent complete above 100% means cost to date exceeds the estimated cost at completion — the estimate was never updated. The cost is real; the EAC is wrong.

weeks.title: Finance U4·W3 — Over/Under Billing, Retainage & the Reclass Entry
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — two numbers that are never the same

A contractor has two completely independent measures of a job’s progress. Billings to date is a contractual event: what the schedule of values and the owner’s payment terms let you invoice. Earned revenue is an accounting measurement: percent complete times contract price. They are never equal, and the gap between them is not an error — it is a balance-sheet account with a name, a normal balance, and real economic meaning.

  • Billed more than earned → billings in excess of costs and estimated earnings, a contract liability. You have taken the customer’s money for work you have not performed. It is deferred revenue wearing a hard hat.
  • Billed less than earned → costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings, a contract asset. You have performed work you have not invoiced. It is unbilled revenue.

Read as cash, the meaning inverts your instincts: overbilling is a source of cash and underbilling is a use of cash. A contractor that is heavily overbilled is being financed by its customers — comfortable today, and a cliff later, because the remaining work must be performed with no billing left to cover it.

The reclass entry

Most construction ledgers record progress billings straight to contract revenue during the month, because that is what the billing system produces. The month-end reclass entry converts that billings-basis revenue to percent-of-completion revenue, job by job. Using the three contracts from Week 2 — earned $4,592,500 against billings $4,634,500:

Overbilled jobs (HR-2, billed $2,900,000, earned $2,762,500):

  • DR Contract revenue   $137,500
  • CR Billings in excess of costs and estimated earnings (contract liability)   $137,500

Underbilled jobs (AC-1 $68,000 plus LR-4 $27,500):

  • DR Costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings (contract asset)   $95,500
  • CR Contract revenue   $95,500

Net effect on revenue: −$137,500 + $95,500 = −$42,000, taking recorded revenue from $4,634,500 to $4,592,500. Three properties of this entry matter. It is computed job by job and only then summarized, because netting at the job level destroys the gross presentation. It is a cumulative true-up, not an incremental posting — the correct technique is to compute the required ending balance in each contract account and post the difference from the existing balance, which makes the entry self-correcting if last month was wrong. And it touches revenue only: cost of revenue is already the actual cost incurred and needs no adjustment.

The trap: billed and earned reversed

This one is embarrassingly easy to make and surprisingly hard to see. The over/under column is built as a subtraction, and the two operands look interchangeable. They are not.

Correct: overbilling = billings − earned revenue. HR-2: $2,900,000 − $2,762,500 = $137,500 overbilled.
Reversed: earned revenue − billings. HR-2: $2,762,500 − $2,900,000 = −$137,500, and if the sign is then dropped or the column is mislabeled, HR-2 lands in the underbilled column.

Now the whole schedule flips. Instead of a $95,500 contract asset and a $137,500 contract liability, the balance sheet reports a $137,500 contract asset and a $95,500 contract liability. Working capital moves from $95,500 − $137,500 = −$42,000 to $137,500 − $95,500 = +$42,000 — an $84,000 swing. Revenue moves the same $84,000, from $4,592,500 to $4,676,500, because the reclass entry runs backwards too.

Two defenses. First, an arithmetic check: total billings minus total earned revenue must equal total overbillings minus total underbillings. Reversed, that check fails in sign — $42,000 versus −$42,000 — and a signed check catches it where an absolute-value check does not. Second, a semantic check: for each job, look at the percent complete and the billing percentage side by side. HR-2 is 65.00% complete and has billed 68.24% of the contract. Billed ahead of complete means overbilled. That sentence takes five seconds per job and cannot be fooled by a formula.

Retainage — and the two ways to double-count it

The owner withholds a percentage of every approved pay application, typically until substantial completion. Meridian’s HR-2 owner withholds 10%. On $2,900,000 of gross billings that is $290,000 retained, with $2,610,000 currently due.

Trap 1 — double-counting the receivable. The correct presentation splits one amount into two lines: contract receivables — trade $2,610,000 plus retainage receivable $290,000, totaling $2,900,000. The error is booking the receivable at the full $2,900,000 and setting up a separate $290,000 retainage receivable, which reports $3,190,000 and overstates assets by exactly the retention. The check is trivially available: contract receivables plus retainage receivable must equal cumulative billings less cumulative cash received. Any workpaper that cannot reproduce that identity has a double count in it.

Trap 2 — using net billings in the WIP schedule. The billings column in a WIP schedule must be gross of retention, because retention is a payment-timing mechanism, not a reduction of the amount billed. Using the net $2,610,000 for HR-2 produces earned revenue $2,762,500 versus billings $2,610,000 — the job reports as underbilled $152,500 instead of overbilled $137,500. The error is $290,000, exactly the retention ($137,500 + $152,500 = $290,000), and it moves a job from the liability column to the asset column, improving reported working capital by $290,000 on one contract.

The mirror image on the payable side. Meridian withholds 10% from its own subcontractors. Subcontractors have billed $1,850,000 on HR-2, so $185,000 sits in retainage payable and $1,665,000 in trade payables. Job cost must carry the gross $1,850,000, because the work has been performed and the obligation exists. Booking subcontract cost net of retention understates cost to date and therefore understates percent complete: cost to date would fall from $2,348,125 to $2,163,125, percent complete from 65.00% to 59.88% ($2,163,125 ÷ $3,612,500), and earned revenue from $2,762,500 to about $2,544,853 — revenue understated by roughly $217,647 on a single job. Retention withheld from a subcontractor changes when you pay, never what the job cost.

Presentation, classification and disclosure

Contract assets and contract liabilities are reported gross: you may not net the $137,500 liability against the $95,500 asset. Sureties and lenders read those two lines against each other precisely because the pattern — large overbillings funding large underbillings — is how a contractor conceals a job in trouble.

Retainage receivable is disclosed separately from trade receivables, and the portion not expected to be collected within one year is classified as noncurrent. That reclassification is not cosmetic: it comes straight out of working capital, and working capital is the number the surety multiplies to set bonding capacity (Unit 6 Week 3). Retainage is also generally not treated as a significant financing component under the revenue standard — it exists to secure performance, not to finance the customer — so it is not discounted.

Finally, an underbilling is a question, not just a balance. Underbilled means work performed and not invoiced, and there are only a few explanations: the schedule of values does not track the actual sequence of work, a pending change order is being performed without an executed contract, the billing was late, or costs have run over the budget on that line. The first two are contract-administration problems, the third is a process problem, and the fourth is gross-profit fade already in progress (Week 4). A controller who reports the underbilling without naming which of the four it is has done half the job.

Reading the overbilling into the cash forecast

The contract liability is not an abstraction; it is a schedule of future cash outflows, and a CFO who cannot convert it into one is flying on the income statement alone. Walk HR-2 forward from Week 2’s facts — contract $4,250,000, EAC $3,612,500, cost to date $2,348,125, billed $2,900,000, 10% retention:

  • Remaining cost to complete = $3,612,500 − $2,348,125 = $1,264,375 of cash to be spent.
  • Remaining billings available = $4,250,000 − $2,900,000 = $1,350,000.
  • Less 10% retention withheld on those billings ($135,000), current cash collectible from remaining work = $1,215,000.
  • Cash gap over the remainder of the job = $1,264,375 − $1,215,000 = $49,375 negative, closed only when the full $425,000 of accumulated retention (10% of $4,250,000) is released at completion.

That is the cliff in concrete terms. The job has been cash-positive to date because it is overbilled; the rest of it is cash-negative, and the recovery depends on a retention release that is contingent on punch-list completion, lien waivers and the owner’s cooperation. Multiply that pattern across a backlog and you have the classic contractor failure mode: growing revenue, comfortable bank balances, and an overbilled position that must eventually be worked off with cash the company does not have. The overbilled balance is the amount of future work already paid for. Put it in the thirteen-week forecast as a scheduled outflow, not as a cushion.

CMA bridge

Contract assets and contract liabilities are Part 1-A External Financial Reporting — unbilled receivables and deferred revenue under the contract-with-customer model, tested as presentation and classification. The reclass entry is a Part 1-E control activity: a computed, reviewed, cumulative true-up posted every close. And the cash reading of over/under billing — customers financing the contractor — is Part 1-B working-capital forecasting, because an overbilled backlog is a scheduled future cash outflow.

Practice and recap

  1. Overbilling = billings − earned revenue (contract liability). Underbilling = earned revenue − billings (contract asset). Always state which operand comes first.
  2. Post the reclass job by job as a cumulative true-up to the required ending balance; it hits revenue only, never cost of revenue.
  3. Sanity-check each job by comparing percent complete to percent billed: billed ahead of complete = overbilled.
  4. Use GROSS billings and GROSS subcontract cost. Net-of-retention billings turned a $137,500 overbilling into a $152,500 underbilling; net-of-retention cost cut percent complete from 65.00% to 59.88%.
  5. Contract receivables + retainage receivable must equal cumulative billings less cumulative cash. Present contract assets and liabilities gross.

Recap: billings and earned revenue are independent measures whose difference is a real balance-sheet account; the month-end reclass converts billings-basis revenue to percent-of-completion revenue job by job as a cumulative true-up; reversing billed and earned flips the balance sheet and swings working capital and revenue by $84,000 on three jobs; and retainage must be presented once and used gross in both the billing column and the cost column, or a single contract can be misstated by $290,000 of assets or $217,647 of revenue.

weeks.title: Finance U4·W4 — Gross Profit Fade, Estimate-to-Complete and the Cumulative Catch-Up
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the estimate is the entire company

Week 2 established that only one number in the WIP schedule is a judgment: the estimated cost at completion. Change the EAC and every downstream figure moves — percent complete, earned revenue, gross profit, over/under billing, the covenant ratio, the bonding capacity. Nothing else in a contractor’s financial statements has that reach. This is why gross profit fade — the tendency of a job’s estimated margin to deteriorate as it progresses — is the single most-watched metric in construction finance, and why the estimate-to-complete process is a CFO-level control rather than a project-management chore.

Fade, measured

Harbor Row Townhomes Phase 2, contract price $4,250,000 throughout:

HR-2 — estimated margin by quarter
Reporting dateEACEstimated gross profitEstimated margin
Q1 (original)$3,612,500$637,50015.00%
Q2$3,697,500$552,50013.00%
Q3$3,782,500$467,50011.00%
Final (actual)$3,825,000$425,00010.00%

Total fade = $637,500 − $425,000 = $212,500, or 5.00 points of margin, or 33.3% of the original estimated profit. That last framing is the one to say out loud to an owner: a third of the job’s profit disappeared, and it disappeared in increments small enough that no single quarter looked alarming.

Fade is a portfolio metric as much as a job metric. Track, every quarter, the change in estimated gross profit on all open contracts, and compute a fade rate: if a contractor consistently fades 3 to 5 points, its estimating system is biased, and every bid it submits — and every forecast the CFO builds on that backlog — is overstated by the same amount. Fade that is random is bad luck. Fade that is one-directional is a systematic defect, and the correction belongs in the estimating department, not the accounting department.

The cumulative catch-up, and how a profitable job posts a loss

Percent-of-completion accounting handles a change in estimate prospectively through a cumulative catch-up: the inception-to-date amounts are recomputed with the new estimate, and the entire difference lands in the current period. It is not a restatement of prior periods. It is a lump, and the lump can be brutal.

At Q2, cost to date on HR-2 was $2,588,250 and the EAC had been raised to $3,697,500.

  • Percent complete = $2,588,250 ÷ $3,697,500 = 70.00%
  • Earned revenue ITD = 70.00% × $4,250,000 = $2,975,000
  • Earned gross profit ITD = 70.00% × $552,500 = $386,750 (check: $2,975,000 − $2,588,250 = $386,750)
  • Prior (Q1) earned gross profit ITD was $414,375
  • Current-quarter gross profit = $386,750 − $414,375 = −$27,625

The job is still profitable — it will finish with $425,000 of gross profit — and yet it reported a gross loss of $27,625 in a quarter in which the crew built a quarter of a townhome complex. Decompose it and the mechanism is obvious:

  • Catch-up on prior progress: prior percent complete × change in estimated GP = 65.00% × (−$85,000) = −$55,250. The 65% already earned had been earned at 15% and is now restated to 13%.
  • Current-period progress at the new margin: change in percent complete × new estimated GP = 5.00% × $552,500 = +$27,625.
  • Sum: −$55,250 + $27,625 = −$27,625.

This decomposition is the CFO’s explanation to a lender, and it is worth memorizing: the quarter’s work was profitable; the quarter’s loss is a restatement of two prior quarters’ margin, recognized all at once because that is what the standard requires. It also explains why late EAC increases hurt disproportionately — the further along the job, the more prior progress there is to restate.

Building the estimate to complete properly

ETC = EAC − cost incurred to date, which at Q2 is $3,697,500 − $2,588,250 = $1,109,250. But that is the arithmetic definition, not the estimate. A defensible ETC is built bottom-up, by cost code, and then the EAC is derived from it — never the other way around:

HR-2 — bottom-up estimate to complete at Q2
ComponentAmountBasis
Remaining committed subcontracts$742,000Executed subcontract value less amounts billed
Remaining self-perform labor$214,250Remaining quantities × burdened crew rate
Remaining material and equipment$108,000Open POs plus unbought quantities at current pricing
Remaining contingency$45,000Unresolved risk items on the risk log
Estimate to complete$1,109,250

Four discipline points separate a real ETC from a wish. Unbought scope is the exposure — committed subcontracts carry price risk only for change orders, while unbought scope carries full market risk, so the ETC must show what fraction is bought out. Buyout savings are not profit until the scope is complete; the single most reliable predictor of fade is a project manager who recognizes early buyout savings and spends them on quality and schedule problems later. Contingency is drawn down deliberately, on a log, with a reason per draw. And the ETC must be reconciled to the schedule: a job forecast to finish in eight weeks that carries sixteen weeks of remaining labor hours has one of the two documents wrong.

The pathology to hunt is the stale EAC — a job where the EAC has never moved off the original budget. It is not evidence of good estimating; it is evidence that nobody is estimating. The classic pattern is an EAC frozen at budget until the job is 90%-plus complete, at which point the accumulated overrun arrives in one catastrophic quarter. A simple control catches it: flag every open job whose EAC is unchanged for two consecutive quarters and require a written re-forecast.

The loss job — recognized in full, immediately

Percent-of-completion spreads profit over the life of a contract. It does not spread losses. When the estimated cost at completion exceeds the contract price, the entire anticipated loss is recognized in the period it becomes known.

Northstar Services holds subcontract NS-19: contract price $640,000, revised EAC $715,000, so the forecast loss is $75,000. Cost to date is $429,000.

  • Percent complete = $429,000 ÷ $715,000 = 60.00%
  • Earned revenue = 60.00% × $640,000 = $384,000
  • Gross profit already recognized = $384,000 − $429,000 = −$45,000 (= 60.00% × −$75,000)
  • Additional provision required now = $75,000 − $45,000 = $30,000

Entry: DR Cost of revenue — provision for loss on contract $30,000 / CR Accrued contract loss $30,000. The accrual is a liability, released as the remaining loss is actually incurred, so no further loss hits the income statement on this job. The asymmetry is deliberate and it is a conservatism principle: profit is earned as performed, loss is a liability the moment it is probable and estimable. Practically, it means a CFO cannot defer a bad job into next year, and a job that flips to a loss position must be reported the same month it is identified.

The four causes of fade, priced

Post-mortem on the $212,500 of fade on HR-2:

HR-2 — fade attribution
CauseAmountOwner of the fix
Change-order work performed without an executed change order$62,000Contract administration
Framing labor overrun (hours, not rate)$48,500Estimating and field productivity
Material escalation on unbought scope$34,000Procurement timing
Extended general conditions from a six-week schedule slip$68,000Scheduling and owner claims
Total fade$212,500

The first line is the one a CFO must stop, because it is pure self-inflicted margin destruction: cost with no matching revenue, recognized the instant it is incurred. Meridian’s rule — no field work on an unexecuted change order without written CFO approval — exists because $62,000 of unauthorized work erased 1.5 points of margin on a job the field thought was going well.

Governing the estimate: who owns the EAC

Because the EAC drives the financial statements, it cannot be a number a project manager types into a field. It needs the same governance as any other significant accounting estimate, and the mechanism is a monthly job review with four fixed rules.

The estimate is proposed by the field and approved in accounting. The project manager owns the operational forecast — remaining quantities, crew productivity, schedule — because that is knowledge accounting does not have. The controller owns whether the resulting number is supported, consistent with the cost ledger, and reconciled to commitments. Neither party should be able to move reported gross profit alone; that is a segregation-of-duties principle applied to an estimate instead of a payment.

Every change is documented with a reason, in writing, at the cost-code level. “EAC increased $85,000” is not documentation. “Framing labor code 06-100 raised $48,500 for 620 additional crew hours at the burdened rate after the rework on buildings C and D” is documentation, and it is also the input to next year’s estimating correction.

Incentives are checked. If project managers are bonused on reported job margin, they are being paid to keep the EAC low, and fade becomes structural. Bonusing on final margin with a holdback, or on forecast accuracy rather than forecast level, removes the conflict. A CFO who complains about fade while paying for optimism is arguing with the incentive plan, and the incentive plan wins.

The forecast is validated after the fact. When a job closes, compare the final actual cost to the EAC at 50% complete and at 75% complete. That comparison, accumulated over twenty jobs, is the company’s estimating accuracy statistic — and it is the honest basis for the contingency the CFO carries in the company forecast and the risk premium built into the next bid. Everything else is opinion.

CMA bridge

The cumulative catch-up is Part 1-A (change in accounting estimate, recognized prospectively in the period of change) and the loss provision is Part 1-A loss-contingency accrual. The fade attribution table is Part 1-D variance analysis in construction dress — separating a quantity variance (labor hours) from a price variance (material escalation) from a scope variance (unapproved change orders). The ETC build and the contingency drawdown log are Part 1-B forecasting and Part 1-C performance management.

Practice and recap

  1. Measure fade as the change in estimated gross profit per job per quarter, and track it as a portfolio rate. One-directional fade is a systematic estimating defect.
  2. A change in EAC produces a cumulative catch-up = prior % complete × change in estimated GP, plus current progress at the new margin. HR-2 Q2: −$55,250 + $27,625 = −$27,625.
  3. Build the ETC bottom-up by cost code and derive the EAC from it. Flag any job whose EAC has not moved in two quarters.
  4. Recognize the FULL anticipated loss immediately: $75,000 forecast loss, $45,000 already in the numbers, accrue the remaining $30,000 now.
  5. Attribute fade to named causes with dollar amounts and an owner for each fix.

Recap: the EAC is the only judgment in the WIP schedule and it controls everything downstream; fade of $212,500 on HR-2 cost a third of the job’s profit in increments nobody flagged; raising the EAC forces a cumulative catch-up that made a profitable job report a $27,625 gross loss in one quarter; a defensible ETC is built bottom-up with unbought scope and contingency shown separately; and an anticipated loss is never spread — it is accrued in full the month it is known.

flashcards.back: The deterioration of a job's estimated margin as it progresses. HR-2: $637,500 (15.00%) → $425,000 (10.00%) = $212,500 fade, 5.00 margin points, 33.3% of the original estimated profit.

Track the change in estimated GP on all open contracts each quarter. Random fade is bad luck; one-directional fade is a systematic estimating bias that overstates every bid and every backlog-based forecast.

A change in EAC is a change in estimate, recognized PROSPECTIVELY: recompute inception-to-date amounts with the new estimate and put the entire difference in the current period. No prior-period restatement.
Current-period GP = (prior % complete × ΔEstimated GP) + (Δ% complete × new estimated GP). HR-2 Q2: 65.00% × (−$85,000) = −$55,250, plus 5.00% × $552,500 = +$27,625 → −$27,625.

flashcards.front: Why a profitable job posts a quarterly loss
flashcards.back: HR-2 will finish with $425,000 of GP but reported −$27,625 in Q2. The quarter's WORK was profitable; the quarter's LOSS is two prior quarters of margin restated at once. Late EAC increases hurt most — more prior progress to restate.

ETC = remaining committed subs $742,000 + remaining self-perform labor $214,250 + remaining material/equipment $108,000 + contingency $45,000 = $1,109,250. Derive the EAC from the ETC, never the reverse. EAC $3,697,500 − CTD $2,588,250 = $1,109,250.

An EAC frozen at the original budget is evidence nobody is estimating, not evidence of good estimating. The overrun arrives in one catastrophic quarter near completion. Control: flag every job whose EAC is unchanged two quarters running.

The FULL anticipated loss is recognized when known — losses are never spread. NS-19: contract $640,000, EAC $715,000 → $75,000 loss; CTD $429,000 = 60.00% complete, so −$45,000 is already booked. Accrue the remaining $30,000: DR provision for loss / CR accrued contract loss.

choices: $212,500, or 5.00 margin points and 33.3% of the original estimated profit

Prior inception-to-date earned gross profit was $414,375. Current-quarter gross profit is therefore:

choices: Unbought scope, which is exposed to full market pricing
questions.explain: Committed subcontracts fix price except for change orders; unbought scope is exposed to the market. A defensible ETC discloses what fraction of remaining cost is bought out.

choices: Nobody is re-estimating, and the accumulated overrun will land in one late quarter
