weeks.title: Finance U5·W1 — Revenue Over Time: The Five Steps Applied to a Construction Contract
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — why the WIP schedule is legal

Unit 4 built the percent-of-completion machinery and took its legitimacy for granted. This week supplies the authority. Under the contract-with-customer revenue model, percent-of-completion is not a special construction exemption — it is what happens when a performance obligation is satisfied over time and progress is measured with an input method. Every column of the WIP schedule maps to a step of the model, and the two places a contractor most often gets revenue wrong — unapproved change orders and materials sitting on site — are both step-3 and step-5 problems.

The five steps on a construction contract

  1. Identify the contract. Enforceable rights and obligations, commercial substance, approval, identifiable payment terms, and collection probable. In construction this is the executed prime contract or subcontract. Two contracts negotiated as a package with a single commercial objective are combined and accounted for as one.
  2. Identify the performance obligations. A distinct good or service, or a series of distinct goods and services that are substantially the same. For a typical building contract, the design-and-build package is a single performance obligation: the individual scopes are highly interdependent because the contractor is providing a significant integration service — the customer is buying a building, not a pile of separately usable trades. That conclusion is what makes one percent-complete measure for the whole contract correct.
  3. Determine the transaction price. Base contract plus approved change orders, plus variable consideration (unapproved change orders, claims, incentives, liquidated damages, penalties) measured and then constrained.
  4. Allocate the transaction price. With one performance obligation, allocation is trivial — all of it goes there. Multiple obligations are allocated on relative standalone selling price.
  5. Recognize revenue as the obligation is satisfied. Over time if a criterion is met, using a single measure of progress.

The over-time criteria — and why a spec home fails them

Revenue is recognized over time if any one of three criteria is met:

  • (a) The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the contractor performs (routine service contracts — landscaping maintenance, janitorial).
  • (b) Performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is created (the ordinary case: building on the owner’s land, or renovating the owner’s building).
  • (c) Performance creates an asset with no alternative use to the contractor and the contractor has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date, including a reasonable margin. Both halves are required, and the right to payment must be legally enforceable at all times during the contract, not just on the customer’s default.

Meridian’s Harbor Row contract meets (b): the buildings rise on the owner’s land, so the owner controls the work in place as it is built. Percent-of-completion follows automatically.

Now change one fact. Meridian builds a speculative house on land Meridian owns, with no buyer under contract. Criterion (a) fails — there is no customer. Criterion (b) fails — no customer controls anything. Criterion (c) fails on both halves: the house has an obvious alternative use (sell it to anyone) and there is no enforceable right to payment for work to date. So the spec house is not over-time revenue. Costs capitalize into real estate inventory and revenue is recognized at a point in time, when control transfers at closing. That is Week 2 of this unit, and it is why a builder can run two completely different revenue regimes in the same general ledger.

The same analysis flips a build-to-suit contract back to over time: a house built on a buyer’s lot under a signed construction agreement, with the buyer controlling the improvements as they are built, meets (b). The determining fact is who owns the dirt and who controls the improvements, not what the building looks like.

Variable consideration and the constraint

Contractors perform disputed work constantly. The transaction price includes variable consideration only to the extent it is probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur when the uncertainty resolves. Estimate it as either the expected value (probability-weighted, useful across many similar claims) or the most likely amount (a single binary outcome), then apply the constraint.

Meridian has submitted a $180,000 claim for owner-caused delay on HR-2. Counsel and the project executive judge that a recovery of $110,000 is the amount that will not later reverse. The transaction price includes $110,000, not $180,000 and not zero. The remaining $70,000 is disclosed, not recognized.

Factors that argue for a bigger constraint: the outcome depends on a third party (an arbitrator, weather, another contractor), the contractor has little experience with similar claims, the range of outcomes is wide, or resolution is far away. The controller’s procedural defense is to keep the claim register — amount claimed, amount included, basis, supporting correspondence — because the auditor will test exactly this in Unit 6 Week 4, and because unapproved change-order cost is being expensed today whether or not the revenue is recognized. That mismatch is the fade mechanism from Unit 4 Week 4, stated in revenue-standard vocabulary.

Contract modifications — and a change order that costs you money

A modification is a separate contract only if it adds distinct goods or services at their standalone selling price. Neither test is normally met on a construction change order — added scope is integrated into the same building, and change-order pricing rarely equals a standalone price. So a construction change order is usually accounted for as part of the existing contract, on a cumulative catch-up basis: adjust the transaction price and the EAC, recompute percent complete, and put the difference in the current period.

HR-2 (contract $4,250,000, EAC $3,612,500, cost to date $2,348,125, 65.00% complete, earned revenue $2,762,500) receives an executed change order for $340,000.

Case 1 — priced at the job’s existing 15% margin ($289,000 of added cost): contract $4,590,000, EAC $3,901,500, percent complete = $2,348,125 ÷ $3,901,500 = 60.19%, earned revenue = 60.19% × $4,590,000 = $2,762,500. Identical to before. Percent complete fell, revenue did not move, and there is no catch-up — a change order priced at the job’s existing margin is revenue-neutral to date. This surprises people, and understanding why is a real test of whether the mechanics are internalized.

Case 2 — priced thin ($323,000 of added cost, a 5% margin): contract $4,590,000, EAC $3,935,500, estimated total gross profit $654,500, percent complete = $2,348,125 ÷ $3,935,500 = 59.67%, earned gross profit = 59.67% × $654,500 = $390,509, earned revenue $2,738,634. Against the prior $414,375 of earned gross profit, that is an immediate −$23,866 catch-up loss, booked the month the change order is signed, before a single hour of the new work is performed. Accepting a below-margin change order dilutes the whole contract retroactively. That is the number a CFO needs before signing, not after.

The uninstalled-materials adjustment

Cost-to-cost assumes cost measures progress. Materials delivered to a site but not yet installed break that assumption: the cost is real, and no work has been transferred. The standard requires an adjustment when the goods are significant relative to the contract, the contractor is not meaningfully involved in producing them (essentially procurement), and control transfers before installation. Then revenue is recognized at the cost of the goods — zero margin — and the cost is excluded from the measure of progress.

Riverton’s utility contract: transaction price $2,000,000, estimated cost $1,800,000, of which a delivered-but-uninstalled equipment package accounts for $200,000 of cost with $200,000 of the price attributable to it. Costs incurred to date are $840,000, including the $200,000 package.

Correct: measure progress on the other costs only. $640,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 40.00%. Revenue = 40.00% × ($2,000,000 − $200,000) = $720,000, plus $200,000 at cost = $920,000. Cost of revenue = $840,000. Gross profit = $80,000, which checks: 40.00% × the $200,000 of margin on the non-equipment scope.

Wrong: include the package in the measure. $840,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 46.67%; revenue = 46.67% × $2,000,000 = $933,333; gross profit = $93,333. Margin is overstated by $13,333 because the contractor took a full margin on simply taking delivery of somebody else’s equipment. Scale that across a mechanical or electrical contractor buying major equipment and it becomes the difference between a good quarter and a real one.

Two more items that belong on every contract file

Warranty. An assurance-type warranty — the work will conform to specification — is not a performance obligation; it is a loss contingency, accrued when probable and estimable. Meridian accrues 1.00% of contract value, so HR-2 carries a $42,500 warranty accrual, released against actual callback costs. A service-type warranty — an extended maintenance package the customer could have bought separately — is a separate performance obligation and takes an allocation of the transaction price, recognized over the service period.

Retainage and financing. Retention withheld by an owner is normally not a significant financing component. Its purpose is to secure performance, not to provide the customer with financing, so the transaction price is not discounted for it. Retainage does, however, drive presentation (a separate receivable line, current versus noncurrent) and it drives the cash forecast, as Unit 4 Week 3 showed.

CMA bridge

This is Part 1-A External Financial Reporting in its most heavily tested construction form: the five-step model, over-time versus point-in-time recognition, variable consideration and the constraint, contract modifications, and contract assets and liabilities. The CMA question that gives you contract price, costs incurred, estimated costs to complete and billings, and asks for revenue, gross profit and the balance-sheet contract account, is precisely the WIP calculation from Unit 4 Week 2 with the authority attached.

Practice and recap

  1. Run the five steps. A typical building contract is ONE performance obligation because of the integration service.
  2. Over time requires meeting (a), (b) or (c). Building on the owner’s land meets (b). A spec home on the builder’s own land meets none and is a point-in-time sale.
  3. Include variable consideration only to the extent no significant reversal is probable: a $180,000 claim included at $110,000, with the rest disclosed.
  4. Treat a construction change order as a cumulative catch-up. Priced at the job’s existing margin it is revenue-neutral; priced thin it books an immediate loss ($23,866 on a $340,000 change order at a 5% margin).
  5. Exclude significant uninstalled materials from the progress measure and recognize them at zero margin: $920,000 of revenue, not $933,333.

Recap: percent-of-completion is the over-time model with an input measure of progress, and its authority runs through the five steps; who controls the asset as it is built decides over time versus point in time; unapproved change orders and claims enter the transaction price only under the constraint, while their costs hit immediately; a change order is a cumulative catch-up that can book a loss before any work is done; and uninstalled materials must be pulled out of the progress measure and recognized at cost, or margin is overstated by the full markup on procurement.

flashcards.back: 1) Identify the contract. 2) Identify performance obligations. 3) Determine the transaction price. 4) Allocate to obligations. 5) Recognize as satisfied. A typical building contract is ONE performance obligation — the scopes are highly interdependent because the contractor provides a significant integration service.

(a) Customer simultaneously receives and consumes as you perform; (b) performance creates/enhances an asset the CUSTOMER CONTROLS as it is created; (c) no alternative use AND an enforceable right to payment for performance to date including a reasonable margin. Any ONE suffices.

flashcards.front: Why a spec home is NOT over time
flashcards.back: Built on the builder's own land with no buyer: (a) no customer, (b) no customer controls the asset, (c) it has an obvious alternative use and there is no enforceable right to payment. Costs go to real estate inventory; revenue at closing. The deciding fact is who owns the dirt.

Include unapproved COs, claims, incentives and LDs only to the extent a significant reversal of cumulative revenue is NOT probable. Estimate by expected value or most likely amount. A $180,000 claim assessed at $110,000 recoverable → include $110,000; disclose the rest.
Rarely a separate contract (not distinct, not at standalone selling price). Adjust the transaction price and EAC, recompute % complete, and put the whole difference in the current period.

flashcards.front: Change order at the existing margin is revenue-neutral
flashcards.back: HR-2 + $340,000 CO at the job's 15% margin ($289,000 cost): contract $4,590,000, EAC $3,901,500, % complete falls 65.00% → 60.19%, earned revenue stays exactly $2,762,500. No catch-up.

flashcards.front: Change order priced thin dilutes retroactively
flashcards.back: Same $340,000 CO with $323,000 of cost (5% margin): EAC $3,935,500, total GP $654,500, % complete 59.67%, earned GP $390,509 vs $414,375 prior = an immediate −$23,866 catch-up loss, booked at signing before any new work is performed.

Exclude significant delivered-but-uninstalled goods from the progress measure and recognize revenue at COST (zero margin). $640,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 40.00%; revenue 40.00% × $1,800,000 + $200,000 = $920,000, GP $80,000. Including them gives 46.67%, revenue $933,333 and GP $93,333 — overstated $13,333.

questions.q: Meridian builds a townhome complex on the owner's land. Which over-time criterion is met?
choices: (b) — performance creates an asset the customer controls as it is created
(a) — the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit
(c) — no alternative use plus an enforceable right to payment
None — this is a point-in-time sale
questions.explain: Building on the owner's land means the owner controls the work in place as it is built. Criterion (b) is the ordinary basis for construction percent-of-completion.

questions.q: Meridian builds a speculative house on land Meridian owns, with no buyer under contract. Revenue is:
choices: Recognized at a point in time, at closing; costs capitalize to real estate inventory
Recognized when the house is framed
Recognized when the house is listed for sale
questions.explain: There is no customer, no customer-controlled asset, an obvious alternative use, and no enforceable right to payment — all three over-time criteria fail.

questions.q: Meridian has filed a $180,000 delay claim; management assesses $110,000 as the amount that will not reverse. The transaction price should include:
questions.explain: Variable consideration is included only to the extent a significant reversal of cumulative revenue is not probable. The remaining $70,000 is disclosed, not recognized.

questions.q: HR-2 (contract $4,250,000, EAC $3,612,500, cost to date $2,348,125) signs a $340,000 change order adding $289,000 of cost — the job's existing 15% margin. Earned revenue to date becomes:
questions.explain: New % complete = $2,348,125 ÷ $3,901,500 = 60.19%; 60.19% × $4,590,000 = $2,762,500. A change order priced at the job's existing margin is revenue-neutral to date.

questions.q: The same $340,000 change order instead adds $323,000 of cost (a 5% margin). The catch-up recorded at signing is:
questions.explain: EAC $3,935,500, total GP $654,500, % complete 59.67%, earned GP $390,509 versus $414,375 previously = −$23,866, booked before any new work is performed.

questions.q: A $200,000 equipment package is delivered but not installed on a $2,000,000 contract with a $1,800,000 EAC; costs to date are $840,000 including the package. Correctly measured revenue to date is:
questions.explain: Exclude the package from the measure: $640,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 40.00%; 40.00% × $1,800,000 = $720,000, plus $200,000 recognized at cost = $920,000.

questions.q: Meridian's standard construction warranty promises only that the work conforms to specification. It should be:
choices: Accrued as a loss contingency — 1.00% of HR-2's $4,250,000 contract = $42,500
Treated as a separate performance obligation with an allocated transaction price
Recognized only when a callback occurs
questions.explain: An assurance-type warranty is a contingency accrual, not a performance obligation. Only a service-type warranty the customer could buy separately gets an allocation.

weeks.title: Finance U5·W2 — Point-in-Time Revenue: Real Estate Inventory, Cost Allocation and the Lot Close
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the other revenue regime

Week 1 ended on a fact that surprises people the first time: the same builder can run two entirely different revenue models in one general ledger. A contract to build on the owner’s land is over time, measured by cost-to-cost. A house built on the builder’s own land and sold when finished is point in time: no revenue at all until closing, with every dollar of cost sitting in real estate inventory on the balance sheet in the meantime. Two houses on the same street, framed by the same crew, accounted for in completely different ways — because control transfers at different moments.

Getting this regime right is mostly two things: knowing exactly when control transfers, and allocating shared development cost to individual lots defensibly. The second is where the money hides.

Capitalize first, recognize later

Under the point-in-time model, costs of acquiring and developing real estate held for sale are capitalized into inventory, not expensed. That includes:

  • Land acquisition — purchase price, closing costs, title, survey.
  • Horizontal development — clearing, grading, streets, storm and sanitary sewer, water, dry utilities, amenity.
  • Vertical construction — the house itself, direct to the lot.
  • Direct soft costs — engineering, architecture, permits, impact fees, builder’s risk insurance, property taxes during active development.
  • Capitalized interest during active development.

Selling and marketing costs and company general and administrative costs are period costs and are never capitalized. Expensing horizontal development as incurred is the classic small-builder error: it understates inventory, dumps cost into a period with no matching revenue, and then makes every lot that closes later look wildly profitable. Neither period is right, and the pattern misleads a lender badly.

Capitalized interest. Interest is capitalized on qualifying assets while development activity is under way, at the weighted-average rate on borrowings, applied to average accumulated qualifying expenditures. Riverton’s Cypress Bend horizontal phase: average accumulated qualifying expenditures $3,200,000, weighted-average rate 8.50%, nine months of active development → $3,200,000 × 8.50% × 9/12 = $204,000 capitalized. Capitalization stops when the asset is substantially complete and ready for its intended use, or if development is suspended. A project that sits idle for a year while entitlements are appealed cannot keep capitalizing interest, and continuing to do so is one of the most common findings on a developer’s first audit.

Allocating shared cost — the relative sales value method

Vertical construction is specific: the house built on lot 12 is lot 12’s cost. Land and horizontal development are shared, and they have to be allocated to lots so that each closing releases the right cost of sales. Riverton’s Cypress Bend:

  • 40 lots: 24 townhome lots at an average price of $400,000 and 16 single-family lots at $550,000.
  • Projected revenue: townhomes $9,600,000 + single-family $8,800,000 = $18,400,000.
  • Shared cost pool: land $2,760,000 + horizontal development $1,840,000 = $4,600,000.

Under the relative sales value method, the pool is allocated in proportion to each product type’s share of projected revenue:

Cypress Bend — allocation of the $4,600,000 shared cost pool
ProductProjected revenueShareAllocated poolLotsPer lot
Townhome$9,600,00052.1739%$2,400,00024$100,000
Single-family$8,800,00047.8261%$2,200,00016$137,500
Total$18,400,000100%$4,600,00040

Relative sales value is the default because it produces a uniform gross margin percentage across product types on the shared cost — the higher-priced product absorbs proportionally more of the land. Two alternatives are also acceptable when they better reflect how the cost was consumed: area or lot-count allocation (appropriate for costs that are genuinely per-lot, such as impact fees and water taps), and specific identification for anything traceable to one lot. What is not acceptable is switching methods to flatter a quarter, or leaving the allocation unassigned until closing and then charging whatever makes the margin look right.

The trap: an allocation that is never trued up

The relative sales value allocation is built on projected revenue, and projections change. When the mix or the pricing moves, the allocation must be revised — prospectively, over the remaining unclosed lots. Closed lots are never restated.

Suppose 18 townhomes have closed at the planned $400,000 average when the market softens and Riverton reprices the remaining 6 townhomes to $355,000, with single-family holding at $550,000.

  • Revised total projected revenue = (18 × $400,000) + (6 × $355,000) + (16 × $550,000) = $7,200,000 + $2,130,000 + $8,800,000 = $18,130,000.
  • Revised townhome share = $9,330,000 ÷ $18,130,000 = 51.4617%, so the townhome pool becomes $4,600,000 × 51.4617% = $2,367,238 (from $2,400,000).
  • $1,800,000 has already been charged to the 18 closed lots at $100,000 each and stays there. The remaining townhome pool is $2,367,238 − $1,800,000 = $567,238 across 6 lots = $94,540 per remaining townhome lot.
  • The single-family pool rises to $4,600,000 − $2,367,238 = $2,232,762 ÷ 16 = $139,548 per lot.

Skip the true-up and the arithmetic simply fails to close: 40 lots at the original per-lot amounts release exactly $4,600,000 of cost, so nothing is obviously wrong on the income statement, but every remaining lot carries the wrong cost and the two product types are cross-subsidized. The margin analysis that tells Riverton which product to build in phase two is then wrong — and that is a real capital-allocation decision made on a bad number. The control is a standing procedure: recompute the allocation at every phase close and whenever projected revenue moves more than a set threshold, and reconcile the unreleased pool balance to the lots remaining, every quarter.

The lot close — when control transfers, and the entry

Control of a completed home transfers when the deed is delivered and the transaction funds — not at contract signing, not at a deposit, not at substantial completion, and not when the buyer walks the house. A signed purchase agreement with an earnest-money deposit creates a contract liability (customer deposit), not revenue. A house that is finished but unsold is inventory, not a receivable.

Cypress Bend Lot 12, a townhome that closed at $412,000 (above the $400,000 average because of options):

Lot 12 — cost of sales build
ComponentAmount
Allocated land and horizontal development$100,000
Vertical construction (actual, specific to the lot)$191,400
Allocated direct soft costs (per lot)$19,500
Allocated capitalized interest (per lot)$11,700
Cost of home sales$322,600

Selling costs at closing (commissions, title, seller-paid closing costs) are 6.00% of $412,000 = $24,720, expensed as incurred. Gross profit = $412,000 − $322,600 − $24,720 = $64,680, a 15.70% margin before company overhead.

The closing entry:

  • DR Cash   $387,280
  • DR Cost of home sales   $322,600
  • DR Selling expense   $24,720
  • CR Home sales revenue   $412,000
  • CR Real estate inventory   $322,600

Debits $734,600 equal credits $734,600. Note the shape of it: revenue and the inventory release happen in the same entry, on the same day, for the same lot. There is no percent complete, no WIP schedule, and no contract asset anywhere in this regime.

Impairment — the point-in-time model’s downside risk

Because cost accumulates on the balance sheet for months or years before any revenue appears, real estate inventory carries impairment risk that a percent-of-completion contract does not. The test is the long-lived-asset test applied at the lowest level with identifiable cash flows — usually the phase or community. If the undiscounted future cash flows are less than the carrying amount, the asset is impaired and is written down to fair value.

Riverton’s phase 3: carrying amount $3,150,000, undiscounted expected cash flows $3,020,000 — below carrying, so it is impaired. Fair value, from a discounted cash-flow analysis using current absorption and pricing, is $2,780,000. The impairment loss is $3,150,000 − $2,780,000 = $370,000, and it is not reversible if the market recovers. The two-step structure catches people: passing the undiscounted test means no write-down at all, while failing it means writing all the way down to a discounted value, so the loss is usually far larger than the amount by which the first test failed.

CMA bridge

This week is Part 1-A revenue recognized at a point in time, inventory measurement and cost allocation, capitalized interest, and asset impairment. The relative-sales-value allocation is also pure Part 1-D Cost Management — a joint-cost allocation problem, structurally identical to allocating joint production costs to products at the split-off point by relative sales value. The prospective true-up is Part 1-A change-in-estimate treatment, the same principle as the cumulative catch-up in Unit 4 Week 4 applied to a different account.

Practice and recap

  1. Capitalize land, horizontal development, vertical construction, direct soft costs and capitalized interest into inventory. Selling and G&A are period costs.
  2. Capitalize interest at the weighted-average rate on average accumulated expenditures, and STOP when development stops: $3,200,000 × 8.50% × 9/12 = $204,000.
  3. Allocate shared cost by relative sales value: $4,600,000 → $100,000 per townhome lot and $137,500 per single-family lot.
  4. True the allocation up prospectively when projected revenue changes: repricing 6 lots moved the remaining townhome lot cost to $94,540 and the single-family lot cost to $139,548, with the 18 closed lots untouched.
  5. Recognize revenue at deed and funding. Lot 12: $412,000 revenue, $322,600 cost of sales, $24,720 selling cost, $64,680 gross profit (15.70%).

Recap: point-in-time real estate accounting parks every cost in inventory until closing, which makes the cost allocation the whole game; relative sales value is the default method and must be trued up prospectively as projections move or product-type margins become cross-subsidized and the phase-two build decision is made on a wrong number; control transfers at deed and funding, not at signing or completion; and because cost sits on the balance sheet for years, the undiscounted-then-fair-value impairment test is a live risk that has no counterpart under percent-of-completion.

flashcards.front: Capitalize vs expense (real estate held for sale)
flashcards.back: CAPITALIZE: land acquisition, horizontal development, vertical construction, direct soft costs (engineering, permits, impact fees, builder's risk, taxes during development), capitalized interest. EXPENSE: selling/marketing and company G&A.

Weighted-average borrowing rate × average accumulated qualifying expenditures, during ACTIVE development only. Cypress Bend: $3,200,000 × 8.50% × 9/12 = $204,000. Capitalization stops when substantially complete or when development is suspended.

Allocate the shared pool in proportion to each product's projected revenue, producing a uniform margin on shared cost. Cypress Bend: pool $4,600,000; TH 52.1739% → $2,400,000 ÷ 24 = $100,000/lot; SF 47.8261% → $2,200,000 ÷ 16 = $137,500/lot.

flashcards.front: When is a different allocation method right?
flashcards.back: Area or lot-count for costs that are genuinely per-lot (impact fees, water taps); specific identification for anything traceable to one lot. Never switch methods to flatter a period.

flashcards.front: Trap — the allocation that is never trued up
flashcards.back: Repricing 6 of 24 townhomes to $355,000 revises total projected revenue to $18,130,000 and the TH pool to $2,367,238. The 18 closed lots stay at $100,000; the remaining 6 take $94,540 each and SF rises to $139,548. Prospective only — never restate closed lots.

flashcards.front: When control transfers on a home sale
flashcards.back: At deed delivery and funding. NOT at contract signing, NOT at deposit, NOT at substantial completion. An earnest-money deposit is a contract liability; a finished unsold house is inventory.

Price $412,000. Cost of sales = $100,000 lot + $191,400 vertical + $19,500 soft + $11,700 interest = $322,600. Selling costs 6.00% = $24,720. GP $64,680 = 15.70%. Entry: DR Cash $387,280, DR COS $322,600, DR Selling $24,720 / CR Revenue $412,000, CR Inventory $322,600.

Two steps: if UNDISCOUNTED future cash flows < carrying amount, write down to FAIR VALUE. Phase 3: carrying $3,150,000, undiscounted $3,020,000 (fails), fair value $2,780,000 → $370,000 loss, not reversible. Failing the first test by a little can mean a large write-down.

After 18 townhomes close at $100,000 of allocated cost each, the last 6 townhomes are repriced to $355,000. Revised projected revenue is $18,130,000 and the townhome pool becomes $2,367,238. The remaining townhome lots should carry:

$78,750 each, after restating the closed lots

questions.q: A buyer signs a purchase agreement on a finished spec home and pays a $15,000 earnest-money deposit. Meridian should record:
choices: A contract liability of $15,000; no revenue until deed and funding
A receivable for the full purchase price
Cost of sales for the completed house
questions.explain: Control transfers at closing. A deposit is a contract liability, and the finished house remains inventory.

questions.q: Lot 12 closes at $412,000 with $100,000 allocated lot cost, $191,400 vertical, $19,500 soft costs, $11,700 capitalized interest, and 6.00% selling costs. Gross profit is:
Riverton expenses $1,840,000 of horizontal development as incurred instead of capitalizing it. The effect is:
choices: Inventory is understated, the development period absorbs cost with no matching revenue, and later lot closings look far too profitable
questions.explain: Neither period is correct — the mismatch dumps cost into a revenue-less period and inflates the margin on every lot that closes afterward.

questions.q: Development on a phase is suspended for a year pending an entitlement appeal. Interest during the suspension should be:
choices: Expensed — capitalization stops when activities necessary to ready the asset are suspended
Capitalized at the incremental borrowing rate
Added to the land basis at closing
questions.explain: Interest capitalization requires active development. Continuing to capitalize during a suspension is a common first-audit finding.

questions.q: A phase has a carrying amount of $3,150,000, undiscounted expected cash flows of $3,020,000, and fair value of $2,780,000. The impairment loss is:
questions.explain: Undiscounted cash flows are below carrying amount, so the asset is impaired and written down to fair value: $3,150,000 − $2,780,000 = $370,000.

weeks.title: Finance U5·W3 — Month-End Close, Cutoff and the GL-to-Trial-Balance Tie-Out
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the close is a control, not a chore

Everything in Units 4 and 5 so far assumed the numbers were complete and in the right period. The close is what makes that assumption true. A construction close has three jobs: get all the cost into the right period (cutoff), prove every balance-sheet account is real (reconciliation), and prove the reported statements tie to the ledger and the sub-ledgers (the tie-out). Skip any one and the WIP schedule — which depends entirely on complete, correctly periodized job cost — is wrong no matter how well the percent-complete formula is built.

The close calendar

A repeatable close is a calendar with named owners, not a heroic week. Meridian’s runs on business days relative to month end:

Meridian Building Group — close calendar
DayTaskOwner
−2Cutoff notice issued; PO and subcontract commitments frozen; field asked for work-in-place estimatesController
+1Payroll posted and burdened; AP entry cut off; bank feeds importedAP / payroll
+2Received-not-vouchered accrual booked; equipment and internal charges postedStaff accountant
+3Bank reconciliations complete; all balance-sheet reconciliations complete; clearing accounts proven to zeroStaff accountant
+4Job cost sub-ledger tied to GL; EAC updates approved in the job reviewController / PMs
+5WIP schedule built; reclass entry posted; statements drafted, reviewed and issuedController / CFO

Meridian’s close ran 14 business days before this calendar existed and runs 5 after. Speed is not the point — a close that takes three weeks produces information nobody can act on, and a management team that has stopped reading a report is worse off than one that never had it.

Cutoff — the accrual that makes construction different

The defining cutoff problem in construction is that work is performed long before it is invoiced. A subcontractor pours foundations the last week of September and submits a pay application on October 6. If Meridian recognizes revenue on cost-to-cost and the cost is not there, percent complete is understated, earned revenue is understated, and the job looks less complete than it is — on every open job, in the same direction, every month.

The fix is a received-not-vouchered accrual built from the field, not from the mail. At September 30, superintendents verified $214,600 of subcontract work in place; vouchered invoices totaled $178,900; the accrual is $35,700, reversed on October 1 as the actual invoices arrive.

Then test it. Meridian samples the first 15 invoices posted in October and checks service dates against the accrual: 3 invoices carried September service dates totaling $22,400, of which $19,600 was already captured. The uncaptured $2,800 is posted, and — more importantly — the pattern is investigated, because a systematic gap on one trade means the field verification is missing that trade every month. The mirror test runs backwards: sample large September postings and confirm the work was actually performed in September, not accrued twice.

Other cutoff points that bite: owner billings (a pay application dated October 3 for September work belongs in September billings), material deliveries (received on site September 29, invoiced October 8), payroll (a week straddling month end must be split by day, not by check date), and equipment and internal charges, which are journal entries nobody chases and so are the most commonly missed.

The tie-out

Three ties, in order, and none is optional:

  1. The trial balance foots and balances. Total debits equal total credits.
  2. GL detail sums to the trial balance for every account. A trial balance is a summary of the detail; if it disagrees with the detail, the export is filtered, dated wrong, or excluding a journal source.
  3. Every sub-ledger ties to its control account.
Meridian — sub-ledger to control account tie at September 30
Sub-ledgerSub-ledger totalGL controlDifference
AP aging$1,482,940$1,482,940—
AR aging$2,317,455$2,331,455$14,000
Job cost inception-to-date$8,946,120$8,946,120—
Retainage payable detail$618,300$618,300—

The $14,000 is an unapplied cash receipt posted to the GL control account but never applied in the receivables sub-ledger. It is named, aged and corrected — not carried as “immaterial.” A difference you tolerate this month is a difference you will not recognize as new next month.

Then the zero-balance proofs. Clearing and suspense accounts exist to hold transactions in flight, and every one of them must read $0.00 at the close, in total. Account 1195 — Interentity Transfer Clearing:

  • Meridian Building Group   $182,400 Dr
  • Riverton Partners   $(176,900) Cr
  • Northstar Services   $(5,500) Cr
  • Net $0.00 — proven.

A clearing account that does not net to zero is an unposted or miscoded leg, and Unit 6 Week 1 explains why the answer is never to eliminate it on a consolidation worksheet.

The trap: a trial balance that suppresses zero-balance accounts

Here is the defect that manufactures work out of nothing, and it is entirely a data-handling problem rather than an accounting one. Meridian’s ledger export omits any account with a zero balance in the period. August’s trial balance therefore has 312 rows and September’s has 298, because 14 accounts that carried balances in August went to zero in September.

The analyst builds the month-over-month variance workbook by pasting the two exports side by side and subtracting row from row. Every row is aligned until the first suppressed account, and every row after it is off by one — then by two, then by three, cascading down the sheet.

Concretely: account 5340 Equipment Rental held $46,800 in August and $0.00 in September, so it vanished from the September export. At that row the workbook now compares August’s 5340 ($46,800) against September’s next account, 5350 Small Tools ($9,240), and reports a $37,560 variance that describes no real event. The workbook flagged 56 accounts above the $25,000 review threshold. Every one was an artifact of misalignment. The four variances that were genuinely worth explaining did not appear on the list at all, because they had been shifted into rows that happened to look quiet.

This trap is dangerous specifically because it looks like diligence. Someone produces 56 exceptions, a team spends a week clearing them, everyone concludes the ledger was fine, and the real movements were never examined. Four defenses, all cheap:

  1. Never join on row position. Join on the account number, with an exact string match — not a fuzzy match, not the account name, which gets renamed and re-spelled.
  2. Use a full outer join and zero-fill. Accounts in either period must appear, with a missing side treated as $0.00. That converts the 5340 case into what it actually is: a real $46,800 decrease, correctly flagged.
  3. Reconcile the account population. 312 August rows minus 14 accounts that went to zero equals 298 September rows. If that arithmetic does not close, the export changed in a way you have not accounted for.
  4. Foot both exports to the GL control totals before either is used. A trial balance that does not foot to the ledger is not a trial balance.

The same family of defect appears in a GL export whose last column is labeled Ending Balance but is period activity — a mix that is especially easy to miss because it is correct for income-statement accounts and wrong for balance-sheet accounts in the same file. Unit 4 Week 1 showed what that does to a percent-complete calculation. The rule generalizes: prove what a column contains before you subtract with it.

Materiality, passed adjustments and the review

Not every difference gets posted. Meridian sets a posting threshold of $2,500 individually, with an aggregate cap of $12,500 across all passed items, tracked on a summary of unadjusted differences that carries forward. Two rules keep this honest. Passed items are listed, not forgotten, so the aggregate can be evaluated and so a difference that recurs in the same direction every month is recognized as a systematic error rather than noise. And a threshold applies to errors, never to unreconciled balances — “the account is off by $1,900, which is below the threshold” is not a reconciliation; it is an unreconciled account with a smaller number attached.

Finally, every reconciliation carries a preparer and a reviewer, and the reviewer’s signature means the supporting detail was examined, not that the sheet was opened. Self-reviewed reconciliations are the single most common control deficiency reported in a small accounting department, and in a three-person office the compensating control is that the CFO reviews the schedules the controller prepares.

CMA bridge

This is Part 1-E Internal Controls almost line for line: control activities, segregation of preparation from review, reconciliation as a detective control, cutoff procedures, and the completeness assertion. The tie-out chain is Part 1-A (how statements are derived from a ledger) and the variance workbook failure is Part 1-F technology and analytics — data quality, join keys, and why an analysis can be arithmetically perfect and completely wrong.

Practice and recap

  1. Run the close on a calendar with named owners and fixed days. Meridian went from 14 business days to 5.
  2. Accrue received-not-vouchered cost from field verification: $214,600 verified less $178,900 vouchered = $35,700. Then test it against October postings and investigate the pattern, not just the amount.
  3. Tie in order: TB balances, GL detail sums to TB, every sub-ledger ties to its control. Name every difference, including a $14,000 unapplied receipt.
  4. Prove every clearing and suspense account to $0.00 across all entities: $182,400 − $176,900 − $5,500 = $0.00.
  5. Join period-over-period data on the ACCOUNT NUMBER with a full outer join and zero-fill. Row-position joins on a zero-suppressing export produced 56 false positives and hid the 4 real ones.

Recap: the close makes complete, correctly periodized cost possible, which is what the whole WIP machinery rests on; cutoff in construction means accruing work in place from the field rather than waiting for invoices; the tie-out is a fixed chain from trial balance to GL detail to every sub-ledger with clearing accounts proven to zero; and the most expensive close-analysis mistake is not arithmetic but a join — a trial balance that suppresses zero-balance accounts will manufacture dozens of false variances and conceal the real ones unless you join on account number and zero-fill.
